Skein Theory for Affine A Subfactor Planar Algebras
Melody Molander

Abstract
The Kuperberg Program asks to find presentations of planar algebras and use these presentations to prove results about their corresponding categories purely diagrammatically. This program has been completed for index less than 4 and is ongoing research for index greater than 4. We give generators-and-relations presentations for the affine A A subfactor planar algebras of index 4. Exclusively using the planar algebra language, we give new proofs to how many such planar algebras exist. Categories corresponding to these planar algebras are monoidally equivalent to cyclic pointed fusion categories. We give a proof of this by defining a functor yielding a monoidal equivalence between the two categories. The categories are also monoidally equivalent to a representation category of a cyclic subgroup of S ​ U ​ ( 2 ) SU(2) . We give a new proof of this fact, explicitly using the diagrammatic presentations found. This gives novel diagrammatics for these representation categories.



1
Introduction

A
von Neumann algebra
is a unital algebra of bounded operators on a Hilbert space closed under a specific topology and possessing an
adjoint
that can be thought of as a generalized matrix transpose. When the Hilbert space is finite-dimensional, von Neumann algebras are necessarily direct sums of the algebras of
n\times n
matrices over
\mathbb{C}
(with varying
n
).
Factors
, which are von Neumann algebras with center isomorphic to
\mathbb{C}
, are building blocks of von Neumann algebras. A unital inclusion of factors,
N\subseteq M
, is called a
subfactor
. The
standard invariant
of a subfactor is the 2-category capturing bimodule data coming from
M
and
N
. When
N\subseteq M
is
finite depth
and both
N
and
M
are the
hyperfinite
II_{1}
factor
, the standard invariant is a complete invariant of subfactors
[
Pop94
]
.

Subfactors have another invariant, a real number called the
index
. Jones
[
Jon83
]
found that the set of all indices of subfactors is the set
\{4\cos^{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{n}\right)|n\geq 3\}\cup[4,\infty]
. Amazingly, techniques used in his proof of this led to the
Jones polynomial
link invariant
[
Jon85
]
and spawned the field of quantum topology.

Subfactor theory can be thought of as a noncommutative version of Galois theory. Whereas Galois theory studies inclusions of fields
F\subseteq E
, subfactors are unital inclusions,
N\subseteq M
, of factors, which are highly noncommutative algebras. Both fields and factors satisfy that any map between them are unital inclusion or zero, so analyzing maps between fields or factors is the same as studying field extensions or subfactors. The index
[M:N]
of a subfactor measures the size of these extensions in a similar notion to the degree
[E:F]
of a field extension.

The standard invariant is analogous to the Galois group. Let
\mathcal{R}
be the hyperfinite
II_{1}
factor and
G
be a finite group. There is exactly one way, up to conjugacy, in which
G
can act on
\mathcal{R}
by outer automorphisms
[
Jon80
,
Con77
]
. Let
N=\mathcal{R}^{G}
, the fixed points of the action.
N
can be shown to be a factor. There will be a Galois correspondence between intermediary subfactors
N\subseteq M\subseteq\mathcal{R}
and subgroups
H\leq G

[
NT60a
,
NT60b
]
. Just like in Galois theory, the automorphisms fixing
N
of
M
,
\text{Aut}_{N}(M)
, equals
G
. Additionally,
|G|=[\mathcal{R}:N]
. However, not all examples of finite index subfactors come from groups.

Decades of work have been done to classify subfactors of small index. For an overview see
[
JMS14
,
AMP23
]
. A
subfactor planar algebra
, introduced by Jones
[
Jon99
]
, is a diagrammatic way to view the standard invariant of a subfactor. 2-morphisms can be drawn as pictures in the plane, reminiscent to braid diagrams. Multiplication of 2-morphisms is given by vertical stacking. Tensor product is given by horizontal concatenation. Existence of some subfactors were proved using subfactor planar algebras
[
BPMS12
,
MP15
]
. The planar algebra framework has opened up a new point of view for the study of subfactors.

Kuperberg posed a program to see how far the planar algebra language can be pushed in the understanding of the standard invariants of subfactors.

The Kuperberg Program:
Give a presentation by generators-and-relations for every subfactor planar algebra and prove as much as possible about the planar algebra using only this presentation.

For subfactors of index less than 4 there is an ADE classification by their
principal graphs
. See
[
Ocn88
]
for an outline of the proof. The Kuperberg program has been completed for all possible indices less than 4. Type
A
subfactor planar algebras are well-understood as the
Temperley-Lieb
planar algebras. Type
D_{2n}
was completed by Morrison, Peters, and Snyder
[
MPS10
]
in 2010. Type
E_{6}
and
E_{8}
presentations were given shortly after by Bigelow
[
Big10
]
.

For index larger than 4, constructing presentations of known subfactors is an ongoing effort. A presentation for the subfactor planar algebras with principal graphs
Haagerup
and its dual was constructed by Peters
[
Pet10
]
and
Extended Haagerup
and its dual was constructed by Bigelow, Morrison, Peters, and Snyder
[
BPMS12
]
. Type
2221
was constructed by Han
[
Han10
]
and types
4442, 3333, 3311, and 2221
were constructed by Morrison and Penneys
[
MP15
]
.

The aim of this paper is to address some of the index 4 subfactor planar algebras. Popa
[
Pop94
]
found that the principal graphs of index 4 subfactor planar algebras are exactly the simply-laced affine ADE Dynkin diagrams. We give the presentations of all affine
A
subfactor planar algebras of index 4.

To satisfy the Kuperberg program, we then use these presentations to prove we have found all planar algebras of type
A
as well as show equivalences to other interesting categories. After finding the planar algebra presentations given in this paper, the author saw similarities to the presentation given in
[
Cze24
]
. In the paper, Czenky gives diagrammatics for cyclic pointed fusion categories,
\text{Vec}_{\mathbb{Z}_{m}}^{\omega}
. The fusion categories
\text{Vec}_{\mathbb{Z}_{m}}^{\omega}
are not strict when the associator
\omega
is not the identity. However, every monoidal category is monoidally equivalent to a strict monoidal category. From the planar algebra presentations we construct in this paper, we show the monoidal equivalence of the nonstrict
\text{Vec}_{\mathbb{Z}_{m}}^{\omega}
to the strict categories coming from the planar algebras explicitly. As a result, this shows how an associator of a fusion category gets concealed in the relations of the planar algebras.

While this paper was in preparation, we discovered that Reynolds’ thesis
[
Rey23
]
also gives presentations of diagrammatic categories with affine
A
fusion rules. However, in
[
Rey23
]
, Reynolds approaches these diagrammatics through the representation theory of a finite subgroup of
SU(2)
. In this paper, we define a functor yielding a monoidal equivalence of these two categories. In particular, we show purely through the defined diagrammatic categories that the category arising from affine
A_{m}
planar algebras, where
m
is finite, is monoidally equivalent to the representation category
\text{Rep}(C_{m}^{\zeta})
, where
C_{m}^{\zeta}
is a cyclic subgroup of
SU(2)
. Both this equivalence and the equivalence to
\text{Vec}_{\mathbb{Z}_{m}}^{\omega}
are known isomorphic categories (see
[
GdlHJ89
]
), however, the diagrammatic proofs of their monoidal equivalences are novel.

1.1
Acknowledgements

The author would like to thank her advisor Stephen Bigelow as well as Dave Penneys for presenting this problem to her, their guidance, and many enlightening conversations.

2
Background

2.1
Subfactors

We begin our background with a discussion on subfactors. We refer the interested reader to
[
JS97
]
for further details. Let
\mathcal{H}
be a Hilbert space. A
von Neumann algebra
is a unital *-subalgebra of
B(\mathcal{H})
,
M
, that equals its double commutant,
M^{\prime\prime}
, i.e.,
M=M^{\prime\prime}
. When the center of
M
is the smallest possible, that is, isomorphic to
\mathbb{C}
, we say that
M
is a
factor
. When
\mathcal{H}
is separable, von Neumann
[
vN49
]
showed every von Neumann algebra,
M\subseteq B(\mathcal{H})
has an essentially unique decomposition as a direct integral of factors. Understanding von Neumann algebras thus boils down to analyzing factors.

There are three types of factors: type
I,II,
and
III
. For this paper, we consider a class of type
II
factors called
type
II_{1}
. A factor of
type
II_{1}
,
M
, in
B(\mathcal{H})
, is an infinite-dimensional factor that admits a normalized trace function. From now on, we use
factor
to mean a type
II_{1}
factor.

To study factors, we consider maps between factors. A factor has no non-trivial closed two-sided ideal, so any map between factors is a unital inclusion or the zero map. Therefore, understanding maps between factors is equivalent to studying a unital inclusion of factors,
N\subseteq M
, which is called a
subfactor
.

There is a special type
II_{1}
factor called the
hyperfinite
II_{1}
factor
, denoted
\mathcal{R}
. Connes
[
Con76
]
proved that if
N\subseteq\mathcal{R}
is a subfactor then
N
is isomorphic to
\mathcal{R}
or is finite-dimensional. In the infinite-dimensional case, since
N\cong\mathcal{R}
, the only information important from the subfactor
N\subseteq\mathcal{R}
is not the von Neumann algebras
N
and
\mathcal{R}
themselves, but their inclusion.

There is a measure of size of a subfactor. The
index
of a subfactor
N\subseteq M
is the von Neumann dimension of
L^{2}(M)
as a left
N
-module
[
Jon83
]
. Remarkably, Jones
[
Jon83
]
found that the possible indices of subfactors lies in the set

\displaystyle\bigg\{4\cos^{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{n}\right):n\geq 3\bigg\}\cup[4,\infty]

and further that every value in this set corresponds to an index of a subfactor. When
M
is irreducible as an
N-M
bimodule, we say the subfactor is
irreducible
.

2.2
Category Theory

For the rest of this paper, we work over the field of complex numbers,
\mathbb{C}
, and assume all subfactors are finite-index and irreducible, unless stated otherwise. We refer the reader to
[
EGNO15
]
for a more detailed study of these topics.

2.2.1
2-Categories and The Standard Invariant

A
2-category
,
\mathcal{C}
, contains objects, morphisms (also called 1-morphisms), and 2-morphisms, which are morphisms between 1-morphisms. See
[
EGNO15
]
section 2.12 for a formal definition. In particular, there are tensor products for 1-morphisms and 2-morphisms under certain compatible criteria. For 1-morphisms, the tensor product is composition. We can tensor two 2-morphisms
f\in\text{Hom}(X,Y)
,
g\in\text{Hom}(Z,W)
as
f\otimes g\in\text{Hom}(X\otimes Z,Y\otimes W)
if
X,Z
and
Y,W
are composable (
X\otimes Z
and
Y\otimes W
exists as 1-morphisms). Diagrammatically, the tensor product is denoted by placing the 1-morphisms or 2-morphisms side-by-side. We can also multiply compatible 1-morphisms or 2-morphisms. In the graphical calculus language, this is vertical stacking:
f\cdot g
is stacking
f
on top of
g
. Additionally, there are associators, and left and right unitors satisfying pentagon and triangle axioms.

Given a subfactor
N\subseteq M
, we can analyze its
N-M
,
M-N
,
N-N
, and
M-M
bimodules. As an example,
N
can be considered as an
N-N
bimodule,
\mathchoice{\mathop{}\kern 7.58473pt\mathopen{\vphantom{N}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 7.58473pt\mathopen{\vphantom{N}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 6.42366pt\mathopen{\vphantom{N}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 6.42366pt\mathopen{\vphantom{N}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}N_{N}
, and
M
can be considered as an
M-M
,
N-M
,
M-N
, and
N-N
bimodule:
\mathchoice{\mathop{}\kern 8.8764pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}{\mathop{}\kern 8.8764pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}{\mathop{}\kern 7.46533pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}{\mathop{}\kern 7.46533pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}M_{M}
,
\mathchoice{\mathop{}\kern 7.58473pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 7.58473pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 6.42366pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 6.42366pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}M_{M}
,
\mathchoice{\mathop{}\kern 8.8764pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}{\mathop{}\kern 8.8764pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}{\mathop{}\kern 7.46533pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}{\mathop{}\kern 7.46533pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}M_{N}
, and
\mathchoice{\mathop{}\kern 7.58473pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 7.58473pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 6.42366pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 6.42366pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}M_{N}
respectively. We can tensor bimodules over the ring between them. For example,
\mathchoice{\mathop{}\kern 7.58473pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 7.58473pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 6.42366pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 6.42366pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}M_{M}\otimes_{M}\mathchoice{\mathop{}\kern 8.8764pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}{\mathop{}\kern 8.8764pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}{\mathop{}\kern 7.46533pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}{\mathop{}\kern 7.46533pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}M_{N}\cong\mathchoice{\mathop{}\kern 7.58473pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 7.58473pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 6.42366pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 6.42366pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}M_{N}
.

From this data we can form a powerful subfactor invariant. The
standard invariant
of a subfactor
N\subseteq M
is a unitary (strictly) pivotal 2-category,
\mathcal{C}
, with
two objects:
N
and
M
. The 1-morphisms are the bimodules tensor-generated by
\mathchoice{\mathop{}\kern 7.58473pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 7.58473pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 6.42366pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 6.42366pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}M_{M}
and
\mathchoice{\mathop{}\kern 8.8764pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}{\mathop{}\kern 8.8764pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}{\mathop{}\kern 7.46533pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}{\mathop{}\kern 7.46533pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}M_{N}
. The 2-morphisms are the bimodule intertwiners. Further, the identities
\text{id}_{N}
and
\text{id}_{M}
are
simple
. (i.e.,
\text{End}(\text{id}_{N})\cong\text{End}(\text{id}_{M})\cong\mathbb{C}
). As the category is strictly pivotal, every 1-morphism
X
has a dual which we will denote
\overline{X}
satisfying that
\overline{\overline{X}}=X
and the properties of duals found in section 2.10 of
[
EGNO15
]
. Since the standard invariant is unitary, this means there is an anti-linear map,
*
, that takes any 2-morphism, say
f\in\text{Hom}(X,Y)
to a 2-morphism
f^{*}\in\text{Hom}(Y,X)
such that the induced inner product
\langle f,g\rangle=\text{tr}(f^{*}g)
is positive definite.

The standard invariant 2-category has diagrammatics that will be used to build the planar algebra. Define
X=\mathchoice{\mathop{}\kern 7.58473pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 7.58473pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 6.42366pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}{\mathop{}\kern 6.42366pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{N}}}M_{M}
and
Y=\overline{X}=\mathchoice{\mathop{}\kern 8.8764pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}{\mathop{}\kern 8.8764pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}{\mathop{}\kern 7.46533pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}{\mathop{}\kern 7.46533pt\mathopen{\vphantom{M}}_{\mathmakebox[0pt][r]{M}}}M_{N}
. We can denote the object
N
by “unshaded” and the object
M
by “shaded”. The generators
X
and
Y
are denoted:

(1)

are 2-morphisms from
X\otimes\overline{X}\otimes X
to itself. We say a morphism is of
type

(k,+)
(respectively
(k,-)
) if there are
k
points on the top and bottom and the region to the right of the star is unshaded (respectively shaded). When the context is clear, we drop the star and the outside box and potentially the boundary of the box itself. Vertical composition (or multiplication) of 2-morphisms is given by vertical stacking. (2)

, where

2.2.2
Fusion Categories

The
M-M
bimodules and
N-N
bimodules give a pair of pivotal categories called the
even parts
. When these categories have finitely many simple objects we say that the subfactor is
finite depth
. In this case, the even parts are fusion categories.

A
monoidal category
,
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,\alpha,\mathbb{1},\lambda,\rho)
is a category
\mathcal{C}
, a bifunctor,
\otimes:\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}
called the
tensor product
,
\mathbb{1}\in\mathcal{C}
the
unit
, and
\alpha_{X,Y,Z}
,
\lambda_{X}
, and
\rho_{X}
the associators, and left and right unitors satisfying pentagon and triangle axioms. A monoidal category is
rigid
if every object has a right and left dual. We say
\mathcal{C}
is
\mathbb{C}
-linear
if for all objects
X,Y\in\mathcal{C}
,
\text{Hom}(X,Y)
has a
\mathbb{C}
-module structure such that composition of morphisms is
\mathbb{C}
-bilinear.

Let
X_{1},X_{2}
be objects in a category,
\mathcal{C}
. If there exists an object
Y
in
\mathcal{C}
, with morphisms
\rho_{1}:Y\to X_{1}
,
\rho_{2}:Y\to X_{2}
,
\iota_{1}:X_{1}\to Y
,
\iota_{2}:X_{2}\to Y
such that
\rho_{1}\iota_{1}=\text{id}_{X_{1}}
,
\rho_{2}\iota_{2}=\text{id}_{X_{2}}
and
\iota_{1}\rho_{1}+\iota_{2}\rho_{2}=\text{id}_{Y}
, we call
Y
the
direct sum
of
X_{1}
and
X_{2}
and denote
Y=X_{1}\oplus X_{2}
. We call
\mathcal{C}

additive
if it is
\mathbb{C}
-linear and for every two objects
X_{1},X_{2}
in
\mathcal{C}
, there exists their direct sum
X_{1}\oplus X_{2}
in
\mathcal{C}
. The category is said to be
semisimple
if every object is a direct sum of finitely many simple objects.

The
kernel
,
\text{Ker}(f)
, of a morphism
f:X\to Y
of an additive category
\mathcal{C}
is a pair,
(K,k)
, where
K
is an object in
\mathcal{C}
and
k:K\to K
is a morphism such that
fk=0
and for any other pair
(K^{\prime},k^{\prime})
satisfying
k^{\prime}:K^{\prime}\to X

fk^{\prime}=0
, there exists a unique morphism
\ell:K^{\prime}\to K
such that
k\ell=k^{\prime}
. The
cokernel
,
Coker(f)
, of a morphism
f:X\to Y
is a pair,
(C,c)
, where
C
is an object and
c:Y\to C
is a morphism such that
cf=0
and for any other pair
(C^{\prime},c^{\prime})
satisfying this criteria, there exists a unique morphism
\ell:C\to C^{\prime}
where
\ell c=c^{\prime}
. An
abelian
category
\mathcal{C}
is an additive category in which for every morphism
\varphi:X\to Y
there exists a sequence

\displaystyle K\overset{k}{\to}X\overset{i}{\to}I\overset{j}{\to}Y\overset{c}{\to}C

such that

ji=\varphi
,
(K,k)=\text{Ker}(\varphi)
,
(C,c)=\text{Coker}(\varphi)
,
(I,i)=\text{Coker}(k)
, and
(I,j)=\text{Ker}(c)
.

A
fusion category
,
\mathcal{C}
, over
\mathbb{C}
is a rigid, semisimple,
\mathbb{C}
-linear, abelian category with only finitely many isomorphism classes of simple objects and the unit object
\mathbb{1}
is simple
[
ENO05
]
.

Given a monoidal category
\mathcal{C}
, we can construct its
additive envelope
,
\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{C})
, which has objects finite formal sums
X_{1}\oplus...\oplus X_{n}
of objects in
\mathcal{C}
and morphisms defined in the following way: for every
X_{1}\oplus...\oplus X_{m}
,
Y_{1}\oplus...\oplus Y_{n}
in
\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{C})
,

\displaystyle\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{C})}(X_{1}\oplus...\oplus X_{m},Y_{1}\oplus...\oplus Y_{n})=\oplus_{i,j}\text{Hom}(X_{i},Y_{j})

and composition of morphisms is given by matrix multiplication.

A
monoidal subcategory
of a monoidal category
\mathcal{C}
is a monoidal category
(\mathcal{D},\otimes,\alpha,\mathbb{1},\lambda,\rho)
where
\mathcal{D}\subset\mathcal{C}
is a full unital subcategory closed under tensor product. For any object
X\in\mathcal{C}
, the
monoidal subcategory generated by
X
is the category with objects
X^{\otimes n}
for all
n\in\mathbb{N}
and is denoted
\langle X\rangle
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\otimes,\alpha,\mathbb{1},\lambda,\rho)
and
(\mathcal{C}^{\prime},\otimes^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime},\mathbb{1}^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime},\rho^{\prime})
be two monoidal categories. A
monoidal functor

\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
is a pair
(F,J)
where
F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
is a functor and
J_{X,Y}:F(X)\otimes^{\prime}F(Y)\to F(X\otimes Y)
is a natural isomorphism such that
F(\mathbb{1})
is isomorphic to
\mathbb{1}^{\prime}
and that the following diagram commutes:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F(X)\otimes^{\prime}F(Y))\otimes^{\prime}F(Z)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(X)\otimes^{\prime}(F(Y)\otimes^{\prime}F(Z))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(X\otimes Y)\otimes^{\prime}F(Z)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(X)\otimes^{\prime}F(Y\otimes Z)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F((X\otimes Y)\otimes Z)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(X\otimes(Y\otimes Z))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha^{\prime}_{F(X),F(Y),F(Z)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces J_{X,Y}\otimes^{\prime}\text{id}_{F(Z)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\text{id}_{F(X)}\otimes^{\prime}J_{Y,Z}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces J_{X\otimes Y,Z}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces J_{X,Y\otimes Z}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(\alpha_{X,Y,Z})}

A monoidal functor
F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C^{\prime}}
is
full
if the induced map
\tilde{F}:\text{Hom}(X,Y)\to\text{Hom}(F(X),F(Y))
is surjective and is
faithful
if
\tilde{F}
is injective. We call
F

essentially surjective
if for all objects
Y
in
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
there is an object
X
in
\mathcal{C}
where
F(X)\cong Y
. The functor
F
is an
equivalence
if it is full, faithful, and essentially surjective. If further
F
is a monoidal functor, we say
F
is a
monoidal equivalence
.

2.3
Planar Algebras

The data of the standard invariant of a subfactor can be equivalently viewed as a
planar algebra
, first defined by Jones
[
Jon99
]
. When
N
and
M
are both the hyperfinite
II_{1}
subfactor and
N\subseteq M
is finite depth, then the standard invariant, and thus its planar algebra, is a complete invariant of the subfactor
[
Pop94
]
. For a more detailed introduction, see
[
Pet10
]
.

A
planar algebra
is a collection of vector spaces with an action of a
shaded planar operad
. The
shaded planar operad
has checkerboard shaded elements which look like:

•

an outer square,
D
,

•

k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
empty inner squares inside of
D
,

•

a possibly empty collection of nonintersecting strands between the squares such that every boundary has the same number of strands on its top and bottom,

•

a distinguished star on the outside of each square.

The below figure is an example of an element of the shaded planar operad.

(3)

Two shaded tangles are equal if they are isotopic. Planar tangles can be composed by insertion under the appropriate conditions. That is, if the shading and number of strands on the boundary agree when the stars match up, we can compose two tangles. As there may be multiple squares in which the composition can be done, we label the squares along with a subscript in the composition indicating which square to insert into. Below we give an example:

\displaystyle\hbox to81.35pt{\vbox to75.18pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 6.77649pt\lower-0.59999pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{}{{}}{}

Notice that the star of each square in a tangle can be in an unshaded or shaded region. We say a square in a tangle has
type

(k,+)
(respectively
(k,-)
) if its star is in an unshaded (respectively shaded) region and it has
k
strands on its top and bottom. For example, the top square in figure (
3
) has type
(3,+)
and the bottom square has type
(1,+)
. The outside square of the tangle has its type defined as done for 2-morphisms in the previous section. So the tangle in figure (
3
) has type
(1,+)
. Composition then is only defined when squares have the same type.

Let
\{\mathcal{P}_{k,\pm}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}}
be a collection of vector spaces. Each tangle can be associated to a multilinear map between these vector spaces. For example, the tangle,
T
, in figure (
3
) corresponds to a map
Z_{T}:\mathcal{P}_{3,+}\otimes\mathcal{P}_{1,+}\to\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
.

Let
T
be a tangle. Then denote
\mathcal{D}_{T}
as the collection of its inner boxes. Define
\partial(D)
to be the type of
D\in\mathcal{D}_{T}
. A
planar algebra
,
\mathcal{P}
, is a collection of vector spaces
\{\mathcal{P}_{k,\pm}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}}
together with multilinear maps
Z_{T}:\otimes_{D\in\mathcal{D}_{T}}\mathcal{P}_{\partial(D)}\to\mathcal{P}_{\partial(T)}
satisfying

1.

isotopic tangles produce the same maps,

2.

the tangle with just straight strands and no boxes is the identity,

3.

the composition of tangle diagrams corresponds to the composition of their multilinear maps.

Define a
homomorphism

\theta:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{Q}
between planar algebras
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{Q}
to be a family of linear maps,
\theta_{n,\pm}:\mathcal{P}_{n,\pm}\to\mathcal{Q}_{n,\pm}
that preserve shading and such that
\theta(Z_{T}(f))=Z_{T}(\theta\circ f)
for every tangle
T
. If each
\theta_{n,\pm}
is bijective then
\theta
is said to be an
isomorphism
.

We define the vector space
\mathcal{P}_{k,\pm}
of a planar algebra
\mathcal{P}
to be its
k
th-box spaces
. When considering the standard invariant, we choose
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}=\text{End}(X)
,
\mathcal{P}_{1,-}=\text{End}(\overline{X})
,
\mathcal{P}_{2,+}=\text{End}(X\otimes\overline{X})
,
\mathcal{P}_{2,-}=\text{End}(\overline{X}\otimes X)
and so on.

2.3.1
The Temperley-Lieb Planar Algebra

The most popular example of a planar algebra is the
Temperley-Lieb
planar algebra,
\mathcal{TL}
. This planar algebra was introduced in 1971
[
TL71
]
and then diagrammatically described by Kauffman
[
Kau87
]
in 1987.

The vector spaces, which we will denote denote
\mathcal{TL}_{k,\pm}
, consist of diagrams of non-intersecting strands with
k
points on the bottom and top and the appropriate shading. Examples of elements in
\mathcal{TL}_{3,+}
were seen in figure (
1
). We also have two elements

in
\mathcal{TL}_{0,+}
and
\mathcal{TL}_{0,-}
respectively.

The generators
X
and
\overline{X}
of 1-morphisms are the same diagrammatic diagrams as the 2-morphisms
\text{id}_{X}
and
\text{id}_{\overline{X}}
, in
\mathcal{TL}_{1,+}
and
\mathcal{TL}_{1,-}
, respectively. In fact, when
P
is a 1-morphism that satisfies
P^{2}=P
, then
\text{id}_{P}=P
. In this case, we often abuse notation and call the 2-morphism
\text{id}_{P}
, just
P
.

The planar operad action on the vector spaces in
\mathcal{TL}
can be seen through diagrammatics. The figure below corresponds to a linear map
Z_{T}:\mathcal{TL}_{3,+}\otimes\mathcal{TL}_{3,+}\to\mathcal{TL}_{3,+}
. Then plugging in diagrams
f
and
g
from (
1
) into the bottom and top squares respectively gives
g\in\mathcal{TL}_{3,+}
, just as shown in (
2
).

This tangle is called the
multiplication tangle (of type
(3,+)
)
. Analogous tangles of all types give that vector spaces in planar algebras can actually be viewed as algebras.

Each algebra
\mathcal{TL}_{k,\pm}
is generated (as an algebra) by a basis denoted
\text{id}_{k,\pm},e_{1,\pm},...,e_{{k-1},\pm}
, where
e_{i,\pm}
has the appropriate shading and is straight strands in all but the
i
and
i+1
position, where there is a cup and cap. As an example,
g
from figure (
1
) is the generator
e_{1,+}
for the algebra
\mathcal{TL}_{3,+}
. The element
\text{id}_{k,\pm}
is
k
straight strands with the appropriate shading.

Another commonly used tangle is the
(right) trace tangle (of type
(k,\pm)
)
,
\text{tr}_{k,\pm}^{R}
, for which we have drawn the
(2,-)
trace tangle below.

Analogous tangles can be drawn for the left trace tangle,
\text{tr}_{k,\pm}^{L}
. We commonly say
the trace tangle
and denote
tr
which means the right trace tangle of the appropriate type. Notice that plugging in any diagram from
\mathcal{TL}
to the trace tangle will result in a diagram in
\mathcal{TL}_{0,\pm}
with no strands on the boundary. We call such a diagram a
closed diagram
.

Two other commonly used tangles are given below.

and

The left-side is the
the dual tangle (of type
(2,-)
)
. We denote the image of a diagram
D
under the tangle by
\overline{D}
. This tangle rotates a diagram by
\pi
. The right-hand side is
the click tangle (of type
(3,+)
).
, denoted
\mathcal{F}
, also referred to as the
Fourier transform
. This tangle “clicks” the star clockwise to the next region, i.e., the star now lies between the top two strands going to the top of the outer box. Analogous tangles of all types exist.

2.3.2
Subfactor Planar Algebras and Their Principal Graphs

A planar algebra,
\mathcal{P}
, arising from a subfactor is called a
subfactor planar algebra
. These planar algebras satisfy a few additional properties:

1.

\mathcal{P}
is
evaluable
: The space of closed diagrams,
\mathcal{P}_{0,\pm}
is one-dimensional. (This means every closed diagram evaluates to a number.)

2.

\mathcal{P}
is
spherical
: the left and right traces of the 1-box spaces are equal (
\text{tr}_{1,\pm}^{R}=\text{tr}_{1,\pm}^{L}
).

3.

\mathcal{P}
is
positive definite
: there exists an antilinear
adjoint map
on each box-space,
*:\mathcal{P}_{k,\pm}\to\mathcal{P}_{k,\pm}
which is compatible with vertical reflection (reflection over a horizontal line) on planar tangles and the bilinear form on
\mathcal{P}_{k,\pm}
induced by the adjoint,
\langle f,g\rangle=\text{tr}(f^{*}g)
is positive definite.

Subfactor planar algebras are a diagrammatic axiomatization of the standard invariant of a subfactor. Jones
[
Jon99
]
proved that given a finite index subfactor, its standard invariant forms a subfactor planar algebra. Using a different axiomatization of the standard invariant called
\lambda
-lattices
, Popa
[
Pop95
]
proved that given a subfactor planar algebra,
\mathcal{P}
, there is a subfactor whose standard invariant forms
\mathcal{P}
. This was then proved using the planar algebra language by Guionnet, Jones, and Shlyakhtenko
[
GJS10
]
.

Subfactor planar algebras encode the index of a subfactor. The value of a closed circle,
\delta>0
, satisfies that
\delta^{2}
is the index of the subfactor. The Temperley-Lieb planar algebra is indeed a subfactor planar algebra as long as
\delta\geq 2
. Any subfactor planar algebra of index greater than or equal to 4 contains a copy of Temperley-Lieb.

By considering a single object in a 2-category, we can arrive at a notion of an
unshaded planar algebra
and
unshaded subfactor planar algebras
. These satisfy all the same properties as planar algebras and subfactor planar algebras, however they are not axiomatizing a standard invariant of a subfactor.

An element,
P
, in any box-space of a subfactor planar algebra satisfying that
P^{2}=P^{*}=P
is a
projection
. From a planar algebra
\mathcal{P}
, we can create a create a 2-category,
\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{P}}
. This category is the additive envelope of the category where

1.

Objects are projections in all box spaces

2.

A morphism in
\text{Hom}(P,Q)
where
P
and
Q
are two projections is any diagram in the planar algebra with bottom boundary
Q
and top boundary
P
.

3.

The tensor product is horizontal concatenation

4.

The dual is rotation by
\pi
(or equivalently
-\pi
)

5.

A projection is
minimal
if
\text{Hom}(P,P)
is one-dimensional. As a consequence, using that
P^{2}=P
, every element of
\text{Hom}(P,P)
is a multiple of
\text{id}_{P}=P
. We say two projections,
P
and
Q
are
isomorphic
if and only if there exists an
f\in\text{Hom}(P,Q)
(giving
f^{*}\in\text{Hom}(Q,P)
) such that
f^{*}f=P
and
ff^{*}=Q
. For any planar algebra,
\mathcal{P}
, the simples of
\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{P}}
are precisely the minimal projections of
\mathcal{P}
. Further,
\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{P}}
is semisimple. This means that the tensor product of any two objects can be decomposed as a direct sum of minimal projections.

In Temperley-Lieb, in each box space,
\mathcal{TL}_{k,\pm}
, there is a unique minimal projection, denoted
f^{(k,\pm)}
, called the
Jones-Wenzl projection
. These projections satisfy that for all the multiplicative generators other than the identity,
e_{i,\pm}
,
f^{(k,\pm)}e_{i,\pm}=e_{i,\pm}f^{(k,\pm)}=0
. These projections have a recursive relation, called
Wenzl’s relation

[
Wen87
]
:

\displaystyle f^{(k,\pm)}\otimes X^{\pm}\cong f^{(k+1,\pm)}\oplus f^{(k-1,\pm)},\text{ where,}

The
n
th quantum number
is defined as

\displaystyle[n]_{q}=\frac{q^{n}-q^{-n}}{q-q^{-1}}=q^{n-1}+q^{n-3}+...+q^{-(n-3)}+q^{-(n-1)}

Then we can define
q
such that
\delta=[2]_{q}=q+q^{-1}
. The Jones-Wenzl projections satisfy that
\text{tr}(f^{(k,\pm)})=[k+1]_{q}
. In particular,
\text{tr}(f^{(1,\pm)})=\text{tr}(X)=\text{tr}(\overline{X})=[2]_{q}=\delta
, and
\text{tr}(f^{(0,\pm)})=\text{tr}(\emptyset_{+})=\text{tr}(\emptyset_{-})=[1]_{q}=1
.

Through the category
\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{P}}
of a subfactor planar algebra, we can view another invariant of subfactors called the
principal and dual principal graphs
. The principal graphs can be though of as a part of a “multiplication table”-like graph that encodes the decomposition of simple objects when tensored by
X
or
\overline{X}
.

Vertices of the principal graphs are isomorphism classes of minimal projections. To find the vertices connected to a vertex labelled by a minimal projection,
P
, we do the following. By the semisimplicity of
\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{P}}
,
P\otimes X^{\pm}
is isomorphic to a direct sum of minimal projections:

\displaystyle P\otimes X^{\pm}\cong\oplus_{Q\in N(P)}Q

(4)

Where
N(P)
is some finite set of minimal projections. Then
N(P)
is the set of neighbors of
P
in the principal graph. The number of edges connecting
P
and some
Q\in N(P)
is the number of times
Q
appears in the summand of (
4
). This means that if
P
and
Q
are minimal projections, there are
\text{dim}(\text{Hom}(P\otimes X^{\pm},Q))=\text{dim}(\text{Hom}(P,Q\otimes X^{\pm})
edges between
P
and
Q
. What this boils down to is that
P\otimes X^{\pm}
is isomorphic to the direct sum of its neighbors in the prinicipal graph.

For Temperley-Lieb, Wenzl’s relation gives that the principal graphs will be the
A_{\infty}
Dynkin diagram:

{f^{(0,+)}=\emptyset_{+}}
{f^{(1,+)}=X}
f^{(2,+)}
…

and

{f^{(0,-)}=\emptyset_{+}}
{f^{(1,-)}=\overline{X}}
f^{(2,-)}
…

This paper deals exclusively with index 4 subfactor planar algebras (which are necessarily of the hyperfinite
II_{1}
factor). In this case, Popa
[
Pop94
]
gives that the principal graphs are the simply-laced affine Dynkin diagrams. Specifically, there are
n
of type
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
for
n\geq 1
, 1 of type
\tilde{A}_{\infty}
, 1 of type
A_{\infty}
(Temperley-Lieb),
n-2
of type
\tilde{D}_{n}
for
n\geq 4
, and 1 each of
\tilde{E}_{6}
,
\tilde{E}_{7}
, and
\tilde{E}_{8}
. For this index, the principal and dual principal graphs are always identical.

To conclude, the decomposition of the planar algebra into minimal projections can be viewed as a
Bratteli diagram
. This is an infinite graph, where row
0
starts at the top.

The vertices in row
k
will correspond to the minimal projections in the decomposition of
X\otimes\overline{X}\otimes\overset{(k-1)}{...}\otimes X^{\pm}
(
k
projections tensored together alternating between
X
and its dual). The labels of the vertices will correspond to the number of times they appear in the decomposition.

The number of edges from the vertex corresponding to
f^{(\lambda,\pm)}
in row
k
to the vertex corresponding to
f^{(\mu,\pm)}
in row
k+1
is
N_{\lambda,\mu}
where
f^{(\lambda,\pm)}\otimes X^{\pm}\cong\oplus_{\mu}N_{\lambda,\mu}f^{(\mu)}
.

We can make the Bratteli diagram for the Temperley-Lieb planar algebra (which we can also call the
A_{\infty}
planar algebra
). Since the principal graph and dual principal graph are the same, we will drop the
\pm
. Using Wenzl’s relation we get the vertices and their labels:

Row 0:

\displaystyle\emptyset\cong f^{(0)}

Row 1:

\displaystyle X\cong f^{(1)}

Row 2:

\displaystyle X\otimes X\cong f^{(1)}\otimes X\cong f^{(0)}\oplus f^{(2)}

Row 3:

\displaystyle X\otimes X\otimes X\cong f^{(1)}\otimes(f^{(1)}\otimes f^{(1)})\cong(\emptyset\oplus f^{(2)})\otimes X\cong f^{(1)}\oplus f^{(1)}\oplus f^{(3)}

Row 4:

\displaystyle X\otimes X\otimes X\otimes X\cong f^{(0)}\oplus f^{(0)}\oplus f^{(2)}\oplus f^{(2)}\oplus f^{(2)}\oplus f^{(4)}

as well as that there will be exactly 1 edge between a vertex in row
k
and
k+1
when the vertices differ by 1. This gives that the first five rows of its Bratteli diagram will look like

1
1
2
1
2
1
3
1
1

From the Bratteli diagram, we get that the dimension of the
k
th box space,
\mathcal{P}_{k,\pm}
, is the sum of the squares of the
k
th row.

3
Necessary Relations for Affine
A
Finite Subfactor Planar Algebras

Our first goal is to find all diagrammatic presentations of subfactor planar algebras whose principal graph and dual principal graph are
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
for all
n\in\mathbb{N}
. Fix
n\in\mathbb{N}
and define
\mathcal{P}
to be a subfactor planar algebra with principal and dual principal graphs the
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
Dynkin diagram. Let
\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{P}}
be the 2-category created from
\mathcal{P}
. Define

(6)

where each
P_{i},P_{i}^{\prime},Q_{j},Q_{j}^{\prime}
for
1\leq i\leq n
and
1\leq j\leq n-1
are representative of their respective equivalence class and the 2 above an edge indicates that there are two edges.

Let
P
be any representative for a minimal projection on a principal graph for some subfactor planar algebra with index
\delta^{2}
. Let
N(P)
denote all the neighbors of
P
in the principal graph. Then taking the trace of both sides of the formula (
4
) gives:

\delta\text{tr}(P)=\sum_{Q\in N(P)}\text{tr}(Q)

(7)

where
\delta>0
. We call (
7
)
the trace formula
.

By Perron-Frobenius, if
\Gamma
is a finite connected graph with vertex set
\Gamma_{V}
, then there exists a function
t:\Gamma_{V}\to(0,\infty)
and a value
d\in(0,\infty)
such that for every vertex
v\in\Gamma_{V}
,
dt(v)=\sum_{w\in N(v)}t(w)
. Furthermore,
d
and
t
are unique up to multiplying
t
by a positive real number. For the trace formula, since
\text{tr}(\emptyset)=1
, the value of
d
is unique, so
d=\delta
, and
t
must equal
tr
in order for
dt(v)=\sum_{w\in N(v)}t(w)
to hold.

Lemma 3.1
.

\mathcal{P}
has index 4 and all minimal projections have trace 1.

Proof.

All minimal projections have exactly two neighbors in their principal graph
\Gamma_{+}
or
\Gamma_{-}
. Therefore, if the trace of all the minimal projections are 1 and
\delta=2
, the trace formula holds. By Perron-Frobenius, these values are unique, so
\mathcal{P}
has index 4 and all minimal projections have trace 1. ∎

Lemma 3.2
.

If
\mathcal{P}
is a subfactor planar algebra with labelling of its principal and dual principal graphs given in (
5
) with
n\geq 2
, then there exists a unique representative of
[P_{1}],[Q_{1}]
in
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
and
[P_{1}^{\prime}],[Q_{1}^{\prime}]
in
\mathcal{P}_{1,-}
.

Proof.

The proof will be identical for
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
and
\mathcal{P}_{1,-}
, so we will just prove the result for
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
. First we prove uniqueness. Suppose
P_{1}^{\dagger}\cong P_{1}^{\dagger\dagger}\cong P_{1}
and
P_{1}^{\dagger},P_{1}^{\dagger\dagger}\in\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
. By the principal graph,
\hbox to16.56pt{\vbox to11.16pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 6.00061pt\lower-0.59999pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{}{{}}{}
{}{{}}{}{}{}{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=1.2pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 M 0 0 L 0 13.78 L 13.78 13.78 L 13.78 0 Z M 13.78 13.78}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {{}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{}{}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{}{}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{}{}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{}{}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{{}}{}{{}{}}{{}{}}{}{{}{}}{}{{}{}}{}{{}{}}{}{{}{}}{}{{}{}}{}{{}{}}{}{{}{}}{}{{}{}}{}{\lxSVG@fill\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -5.51 8.45 L -6.66 7.09 L -8.3 6.42 L -7.37 4.91 L -7.24 3.14 L -5.51 3.56 L -3.79 3.14 L -3.65 4.91 L -2.72 6.42 L -4.36 7.09 Z}{stroke:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@transformcm{0.3}{0.0}{0.0}{0.3}{-3.98329pt}{3.98329pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform=matrix(0.3 0.0 0.0 0.3 -5.51 5.51)} \pgfsys@hbox{59}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{}}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\otimes X\cong X\cong P_{1}\oplus Q_{1}
. By definition of direct sum, there exists morphisms in
\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{P}}
,
\rho_{1}:P_{1}\oplus Q_{1}\rightarrow P_{1}
,
\rho_{2}:P_{1}\oplus Q_{1}\rightarrow Q_{1}
,
\iota_{1}:P_{1}\rightarrow P_{1}\oplus Q_{1}
, and
\iota_{2}:Q_{1}\rightarrow P_{1}\oplus Q_{1}
, satisfying
\rho_{1}\iota_{1}=\text{id}_{P_{1}}
,
\rho_{2}\iota_{2}=\text{id}_{Q_{1}}
,
\rho_{2}\iota_{1}=\rho_{1}\iota_{2}=0
and
\iota_{1}\rho_{1}+\iota_{2}\rho_{2}=\text{id}_{P_{1}\oplus Q_{1}}
. By definition of isomorphism there exists morphisms in
\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{P}}
,
f:P_{1}\oplus Q_{1}\rightarrow X
,
g:X\rightarrow P_{1}\oplus Q_{1}
such that
fg=\text{id}_{X}
and
gf=\text{id}_{P_{1}\oplus Q_{1}}
. Thus

f\text{id}_{P_{1}\oplus Q_{1}}g=fg=\text{id}_{X}=f\iota_{1}\rho_{1}g+f\iota_{2}\rho_{2}g

(8)

Call the map
R=f\iota_{1}\rho_{1}g\in\text{Hom}\left(X,X\right)
and
S=f\iota_{2}\rho_{2}g\in\text{Hom}\left(X,X\right)
, so we can rewrite (
8
) as
\text{id}_{X}=R+S
. Since
P_{1}^{\dagger}\in\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
and is a projection,
\text{id}_{X}P_{1}^{\dagger}\text{id}_{X}=P_{1}^{\dagger}\in\text{Hom}(X,X)
. On the other hand, using that
\text{id}_{X}=R+S
we get

P_{1}^{\dagger}=(R+S)P_{1}^{\dagger}(R+S)=RP_{1}^{\dagger}R+RP_{1}^{\dagger}S+SP_{1}^{\dagger}R+SP_{1}^{\dagger}S

(9)

S
is a map that factors through
Q_{1}
and not
P_{1}
and as
Q_{1}
and
P_{1}^{\dagger}
are nonisomorphic minimal projections
RP_{1}^{\dagger}S=SP_{1}^{\dagger}R=SP_{1}^{\dagger}S=0
. What’s left to compute is
RP_{1}^{\dagger}R=f\iota_{1}\rho_{1}gP_{1}^{\dagger}f\iota_{1}\rho_{1}g
. Notice that
\rho_{1}gP_{1}^{\dagger}f\iota_{1}\in\text{Hom}(P_{1},P_{1})
and as this hom-space is one-dimensional, this gives that
\rho_{1}gP_{1}^{\dagger}f\iota_{1}=\lambda P_{1}
for some
\lambda\in\mathbb{C}
. Equation (
9
) becomes
RP_{1}^{\dagger}R=\lambda(f\iota_{1}\rho_{1}g)=\lambda R=P_{1}^{\dagger}
. We can deduce that
\lambda
is nonzero since
P_{1}^{\dagger}
has nonzero trace. We can do the same thing for
P_{1}^{\dagger\dagger}
and get that there exists a
\mu\in\mathbb{C}\backslash\{0\}
such that
\mu R=P_{1}^{\dagger\dagger}
. Thus
\frac{1}{\lambda}P_{1}^{\dagger}=\frac{1}{\mu}P_{1}^{\dagger\dagger}
.
P_{1}^{\dagger}
and
P_{1}^{\dagger\dagger}
have the same trace, so
\frac{1}{\lambda}\text{tr}(P_{1}^{\dagger})=\frac{1}{\mu}\text{tr}(P_{1}^{\dagger\dagger})
, giving that
\lambda=\mu
and
P_{1}^{\dagger}=P_{1}^{\dagger\dagger}
, proving uniqueness. A similar proof will show uniqueness for the representative of
[Q_{1}]
in
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
.

Next, we prove existence. We claim that
R
is the correct choice for the unique representative
[P_{1}]
in
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
and
S
is the correct choice for the unique representative of
[Q_{1}]
in
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
. It easy to see that
R^{2}=R
. As
R\in\text{Hom}\left(X,X\right)
,
R\in\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
. What’s left to show is that
R\cong P_{1}
. Defining
h_{1}=\rho_{1}g\in\text{Hom}\left(X,P_{1}\right)
and
k_{1}=f\iota_{1}\in\text{Hom}\left(P_{1},X\right)
gives
R\cong P_{1}
. So indeed
R
is the unique representative of
[P_{1}]
in
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
. A similar proof shows
S
is the unique representative of
[Q_{1}]
in
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
. ∎

Lemma 3.3
.

When
n=1
, there exists
R_{1},Q_{1}\in\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
isomorphic to
P_{1}
and
R_{1}^{\prime},Q_{1}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}_{1,-}
isomorphic to
P_{1}^{\prime}
with
R_{1}Q_{1}=Q_{1}R_{1}=0
,
\overline{R}_{1}\overline{Q}_{1}=\overline{Q}_{1}\overline{R}_{1}=0
,
X=R_{1}+Q_{1}
,
Y=R_{1}^{\prime}+Q_{1}^{\prime}
and
\overline{R}_{1}=R_{1}^{\prime}
and
\overline{Q}_{1}=Q_{1}^{\prime}
.

Proof.

When
n=1
, the principal graph gives that
X\cong P_{1}\oplus P_{1}
. By definition of direct sum, this means that there exists some
R_{1},Q_{1}\in\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
with
R_{1}Q_{1}=Q_{1}R_{1}=0
and
X=R_{1}+Q_{1}
. Taking the duals of
R_{1}
and
Q_{1}
we get
\overline{R}_{1}\overline{Q}_{1}=\overline{Q}_{1}\overline{R}_{1}=0
and
Y=\overline{R}_{1}+\overline{Q}_{1}
and
\overline{R}_{1},\overline{Q}_{1}\in\mathcal{P}_{1,-}
. Since
R_{1}
and
Q_{1}
are minimal projections isomorphic to
P_{1}
this gives that
\overline{R}_{1}
and
\overline{Q}_{1}
are minimal projections. Since
Y=\overline{R}_{1}+\overline{Q}_{1}
we obtain that
\overline{R}_{1}\cong\overline{Q}_{1}\cong P_{1}^{\prime}
. ∎

From now on, for
n\geq 2
, choose
P_{1}
and
Q_{1}
to be the unique representatives of
[P_{1}]
and
[Q_{1}]
in
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
and let
P_{1}^{\prime}
,
Q_{1}^{\prime}
be the unique representatives of
[P_{1}^{\prime}]
and
[Q_{1}^{\prime}]
in
\mathcal{P}_{1,-}
respectively. For
n=1
choose
P_{1}=R_{1}
,
P_{1}^{\prime}=\overline{R}_{1}
,
Q_{1}
, and
Q_{1}^{\prime}=\overline{Q}_{1}
from Lemma
3.3
. From Lemmas
3.3
and
3.2
,
X=P_{1}+Q_{1}
and
Y=P_{1}^{\prime}+Q_{1}^{\prime}
. We already know when
n=1
that we can asssume
P_{1}^{\prime}=\overline{P}_{1}
and
Q_{1}^{\prime}=\overline{Q}_{1}
. We prove this result for
n\geq 2
by first finding bases for
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
and
\mathcal{P}_{1,-}
.

Lemma 3.4
.

For
n\geq 2
,
\{P_{1},Q_{1}\}
forms a basis of
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
and
\{P_{1}^{\prime},Q_{1}^{\prime}\}
forms a basis of
\mathcal{P}_{1,-}
.

Proof.

Without loss of generality, we will show
\{P_{1},Q_{1}\}
forms a basis of
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
. Recall from the background discussion that the dimension of
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
is the sums of the squares in row 1 of the Brattelli diagram. Since
X\cong P_{1}\oplus Q_{1}
, the dimension of
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
is 2.

What’s left to check is that
P_{1}
and
Q_{1}
are linearly independent. Since
Q_{1}
and
P_{1}
are nonisomorphic minimal projections, neither
Q_{1}
or
P_{1}
are zero and
P_{1}Q_{1}=Q_{1}P_{1}=0
,
P_{1}^{2}=P_{1}
, and
Q_{1}^{2}=Q_{1}
. Therefore if there exists
\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb{C}
where
\lambda P_{1}+\mu Q_{1}=0
, multiplying by
P_{1}
gives
\lambda=0
and multiplying by
Q_{1}
gives
\mu=0
. ∎

Lemma 3.5
.

Either
\overline{P}_{1}=P_{1}^{\prime}
and
\overline{Q}_{1}=Q_{1}^{\prime}
or
\overline{P}_{1}=Q_{1}^{\prime}
and
\overline{Q}_{1}=P_{1}^{\prime}
.

Proof.

The case
n=1
was done in Lemma
3.3
. In Lemma
3.2
we found that
P_{1}
and
Q_{1}
satisfy
X=P_{1}+Q_{1}
and that
Y=P_{1}^{\prime}+Q_{1}^{\prime}
. By definition of projection,
P_{1}^{2}=P_{1}=P_{1}^{*}
. For any diagram
A\in\mathcal{P}
it is clear that
\overline{A}^{2}=\overline{A^{2}}
and
\overline{A}^{*}=\overline{A^{*}}
, thus

\displaystyle\overline{P_{1}^{2}}=\overline{P}_{1}=\overline{P}_{1}^{2}=\overline{P_{1}^{*}}=\overline{P}_{1}^{*}

which gives that
\overline{P}_{1}\in\mathcal{P}_{1,-}
is a projection. Similarly,
\overline{Q}_{1}\in\mathcal{P}_{1,-}
is a projection.

Let
R
be any minimal projection. Clearly,
f\in\text{Hom}(P_{1},R)
if and only if
\overline{f}\in\text{Hom}(\overline{R},\overline{P}_{1})
, which gives that the dimension of the hom-space from
\overline{P}_{1}
to itself is 1 and from
\overline{P}_{1}
to any nonisomorphic minimal projection is 0. Thus,
\overline{P}_{1}
is a minimal projection in
\mathcal{P}_{1,-}
. By Lemma
3.2
this gives that
\overline{P}_{1}=P_{1}^{\prime}
or
\overline{P}_{1}=Q_{1}^{\prime}
. Likewise,
\overline{Q}_{1}
is a minimal projection. The dimension of
\text{Hom}(\overline{P}_{1},\overline{Q}_{1})
is 0 since
\text{Hom}(P_{1},Q_{1})
has dimension 0, so
\overline{P}_{1}
and
\overline{Q}_{1}
are nonisomorphic minimal projections. Therefore, either
\overline{P}_{1}=P_{1}^{\prime}
and
\overline{Q}_{1}=Q_{1}^{\prime}
or
\overline{P}_{1}=Q_{1}^{\prime}
and
\overline{Q}_{1}=P_{1}^{\prime}
. ∎

Due to the principal graph’s symmetry we can choose that
\overline{P}_{1}=P_{1}^{\prime}
and
\overline{Q}_{1}=Q_{1}^{\prime}
. Recall that in a planar algebra, the dual of a diagram is rotation by
\pi
. For our diagrammatic descriptions of subfactor planar algebras with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
, we will want to have diagrams
P_{1}
,
P_{1}^{\prime}
,
Q_{1}
,
Q_{1}^{\prime}
such that
P_{1},Q_{1}\in\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
,
P_{1}^{\prime},Q_{1}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}_{1,-}
, and rotating
P_{1}
and
Q_{1}

\pi
gives
P_{1}^{\prime}
and
Q_{1}^{\prime}
respectively. We will introduce diagrammatic notation that aids the visualization of this phenomena by denoting

Thus we can conclude
P_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\cong\emptyset_{+}\cong Q_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\cong\emptyset_{+}
and
\overline{P}_{1}\otimes P_{1}\cong\emptyset_{-}\cong\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}
.

Proof.

We will prove the first equality or isomorphism of each part. The rest will follow analogously. Define
D
to be the lefthand side of the first equality of part (i). For part (i), using that the trace of
P_{1}
and
\overline{P}_{1}
are 1, we can see that

\displaystyle\Biggl<D-(P_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}),D-(P_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1})\Biggr>=\text{tr}\left(-D+(P_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1})\right)=0

Since
\mathcal{P}
is a subfactor planar algebra, the inner product
<,>
is positive-definite, which gives that
D-(P_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1})=0
and thus
D=P_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}
.

Using the previous lemma and its proof we can see that for any diagram
T
in the planar algebra,
T^{*}
is vertical flip and star the inside of any box, then extend this definition anti-linearly and on diagrams.

Lemma 3.7
.

In
\mathcal{P}
,
\text{tr}(X)=2\emptyset_{+}
and
\text{tr}(Y)=2\emptyset_{-}
.

Proof.

This follows immediately from taking the traces of the identities:
X=P_{1}+Q_{1}
and
Y=\overline{P}_{1}+\overline{Q}_{1}
. ∎

Lemma 3.8
.

Let
n\geq 2
. In
\mathcal{P}
with principal graphs given by (
5
) we get:

(i)

P_{k}\cong P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes P_{1}\otimes\overset{(k-2)}{...}\otimes R_{1}
,

(ii)

P_{k}^{\prime}\cong\overline{P}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\overset{(k-2)}{...}\otimes\overline{R}_{1}
,

(iii)

Q_{\ell}\cong Q_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes\overset{(\ell-2)}{...}\otimes\overline{R}_{2}
, and

(iv)

Q_{\ell}^{\prime}\cong\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\overset{(\ell-2)}{...}\otimes R_{2}

for
1\leq k\leq n
and
1\leq\ell\leq n-1
where
R_{1}
and
R_{2}
are either
P_{1}
or
\overline{Q}_{1}
, depending on the parity of
n
, and
R_{1}\neq R_{2}
.

Proof.

Proving each part is nearly identical, so we will just prove (i). We will prove (i) by induction. When
k=1
, the claim is clear. By the principal graph,
P_{1}\otimes Y\cong\emptyset_{+}\oplus P_{2}
. In Lemma
3.2
we showed
X=P_{1}+Q_{1}
, so we get
Y=\overline{P}_{1}+\overline{Q}_{1}
. Then

\displaystyle P_{1}\otimes Y=P_{1}\otimes(\overline{P}_{1}+\overline{Q}_{1})=P_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}+P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}.

By Lemma
3.6
we know
P_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\cong\emptyset_{+}
, which gives
P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\cong P_{2}
.

Next, assume the claim is true up to some
2\leq k\leq n-1
. When
k
is even,
R_{1}=\overline{Q}_{1}
, that is,
P_{k}\cong P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes\overset{(k-1)}{...}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}
. Then, by the principal graph,
P_{k}\otimes X\cong P_{k-1}\oplus P_{k+1}
. Since
X=P_{1}+Q_{1}
, we get that

\displaystyle P_{k}\otimes X=P_{k}\otimes(P_{1}+Q_{1})=P_{k}\otimes P_{1}+P_{k}\otimes Q_{1}\cong P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes\overset{(k-1)}{...}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes P_{1}+P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes\overset{(k-1)}{...}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}

and again, from Lemma
3.6
, we know
\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}\cong\emptyset_{-}
, which gives
P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes\overset{(k-2)}{...}\otimes P_{1}\cong P_{k-1}
. Therefore,
P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes\overset{(k-1)}{...}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes P_{1}\cong P_{k+1}
, as desired.

When
k
is odd,
R_{1}=P_{1}
, so
P_{k}\cong P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes\overset{(k-1)}{...}\otimes P_{1}
. By the principal graph,
P_{k}\otimes Y\cong P_{k-1}\oplus P_{k+1}
. Since
Y=\overline{P}_{1}+\overline{Q}_{1}
, we get

\displaystyle P_{k}\otimes Y\cong P_{k}\otimes(\overline{P}_{1}+\overline{Q}_{1})=P_{k}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}+P_{k}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\cong P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes\overset{(k-1)}{...}\otimes P_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}+P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes\overset{(k-1)}{...}\otimes P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}

As
P_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\cong\emptyset_{+}
, we get
P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes\overset{(k-1)}{...}\otimes P_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\cong P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes\overset{(k-2)}{...}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\cong P_{k-1}
, we get
P_{k+1}\cong P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes\overset{(k-1)}{...}\otimes P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}
. Hence, we have the desired claim. ∎

Lemma 3.9
.

Let
n\geq 2
. In
\mathcal{P}
with principal graphs given by (
5
) we get:

(i)

P_{n}\cong Q_{n-1}\otimes\overline{R}_{2}

(ii)

P_{n}^{\prime}\cong Q_{n-1}\otimes R_{2}

where
R_{2}
is
P_{1}
or
\overline{Q}_{1}
, depending on the parity of
n
.

Proof.

Both parts will be similar, so we just prove part (i). First assume
n
is even. So
\overline{R}_{2}=\overline{P}_{1}
. By the principal graph,
Q_{n-1}\otimes Y\cong Q_{n-2}\oplus P_{n}
. On the other hand, from Lemma
3.8
and the fact that
Y=\overline{P}_{1}+\overline{Q}_{1}
we obtain,

\displaystyle Q_{n-1}\otimes Y\cong Q_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes\overset{(n-3)}{...}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes Y\cong Q_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes\overset{(n-3)}{...}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}+Q_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes\overset{(n-3)}{...}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}

Since
Q_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\cong\emptyset_{+}
, we have that

\displaystyle Q_{1}\otimes\overset{(n-3)}{...}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\cong Q_{1}\otimes\overset{(n-4)}{...}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\cong Q_{n-2}

which gives then that
P_{n}\cong Q_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes\overset{(n-3)}{...}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}
, as we wished.

When
n
is odd,
\overline{R}_{2}=Q_{1}
. The principal graph nows gives
Q_{n-1}\otimes X\cong Q_{n-2}\oplus P_{n}
. Similar to the even case, using that
X=P_{1}+Q_{1}
, we get

\displaystyle Q_{n-1}\otimes X\cong Q_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes\overset{(n-3)}{...}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\otimes X\cong Q_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes\overset{(n-3)}{...}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\otimes P_{1}+Q_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes\overset{(n-3)}{...}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}.

Since
\overline{P}_{1}\otimes P_{1}\cong\emptyset_{-}
, we get
Q_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes\overset{(n-4)}{...}\otimes Q_{1}\cong Q_{n-2}

which then gives that
P_{n}\cong Q_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes\overset{(n-3)}{...}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}
, completing the proof. ∎

We are now ready to prove the necessary relations for any subfactor planar algebra with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
. For diagrams
U
,
U^{*}
,
V
, and
V^{*}
we intend to indicate that the strands are alternating in color. A purple strand indicates a strand of color blue or red. We also intend for these diagrams to have checkerboard shading. We shade the regions that must be shaded and use a “checkerboard” to indicate a region that should have the appropriate shading, which will depend on
n
.

(Elements in Affine
A
Subfactor Planar Algebras)
.

\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
subfactor planar algebras have elements

\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}
{}{{}}{}{}{}{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#808080} \lxSVG@stroke@opacity{0.5}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-opacity=0.5} \lxSVG@fill@opacity{0.5}\lxSVG@begingroup@{fill-opacity=0.5} \lxSVG@fill\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 14.61 0 M 14.61 0 L 14.61 27.56 L 27.56 27.56 L 27.56 0 Z M 27.56 27.56}{stroke:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

We now show that the elements and relations defined above are necessarily elements and relations in an
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
subfactor planar algebra.

Theorem 3.10
.

(Necessary relations for
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
). Fix
n\in\mathbb{N}
. If
\mathcal{P}
is a subfactor planar algebra with principal graph and dual principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
, then
\mathcal{P}
has the elements from Definition (
3.1
) and relations from Definition (
3.2
). Further, we get the equivalence classes of minimial projections are when
n\geq 2
:

\Gamma_{+}:\hbox to180.4pt{\vbox to116.6pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 22.92613pt\lower-54.08524pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}

Therefore there exists morphisms
U
,
U^{*}
,
W
, and
W^{*}
in
\mathcal{P}
such that
U\in\text{Hom}(Q_{n},P_{n})
,
U^{*}\in\text{Hom}(P_{n},Q_{n}),W\in\text{Hom}(Q_{n}^{\prime},P_{n}^{\prime})
, and
W^{*}\in\text{Hom}(P_{n}^{\prime},Q_{n}^{\prime})
, such that
UU^{*}=\text{id}_{P_{n}}=P_{n}
,
U^{*}U=\text{id}_{Q_{n}}=Q_{n}
,
WW^{*}=\text{id}_{P_{n}^{\prime}}=P_{n}^{\prime}
, and
W^{*}W=\text{id}_{Q_{n}^{\prime}}=Q_{n}^{\prime}
, where the second equalities of all of these is due to
P_{n}
,
P_{n}^{\prime}
(and thus
Q_{n}
and
Q_{n}^{\prime}
) being projections. Diagrammatically, this means there are elements

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{}}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\text{ }

in
\mathcal{P}
and further, they satisfy relation (v).

Next, note that
\mathcal{F}(U)\in\text{Hom}(P_{n}^{\prime},Q_{n}^{\prime})
, and since
Q_{n}^{\prime}\cong P_{n}^{\prime}
, this hom-space is one-dimensional. Therefore there is an
\alpha\in\mathbb{C}
such that
\mathcal{F}(U)=\alpha W^{*}
. Similarly, there exists a
\beta\in\mathbb{C}
where
\mathcal{F}(W^{*})=\beta U
. Taking
\mathcal{F}^{-1}
of both sides of each equation and moving the scalar the other side gives
\alpha^{-1}U=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(W^{*})
and
\beta^{-1}W^{*}=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(U)
. Taking the adjoint of both sides, which is vertically flipping and interchanging
U
and
U^{*}
as well as
W
and
W^{*}
, gives
\mathcal{F}^{-1}(U^{*})=\overline{\alpha}W
and
\mathcal{F}^{-1}(W)=\overline{\beta}U^{*}
. Applying the click again, we obtain
\mathcal{F}(W)=\overline{\alpha}^{-1}U^{*}
and
\mathcal{F}(U^{*})=\overline{\beta}^{-1}W
. Since
\mathcal{F}(U)=\alpha W^{*}
,
\mathcal{F}^{2}(U)=\alpha\mathcal{F}(W^{*})=\alpha\beta U
. Then because
\mathcal{F}^{2n}
is the identity map,
\mathcal{F}^{2n}(U)=(\alpha\beta)^{n}(U)
. So
\alpha\beta
is an
n
th root of unity. Define
\sigma_{n}=\alpha\beta

V=\beta W
, and
V^{*}=\overline{\beta}W^{*}
, and diagrammatically denote these as

V
…
(n-1)
…
(n-1)

and
V^{*}
…
(n-1)
…
(n-1)

Next we show that
V
and
V^{*}
satisfy the requirements of relation (iv). To do so, we first show that
\overline{\beta}=\beta^{-1}
. This is true since, using sphericality, we can move the rightmost strand of
\text{tr}(UU^{*})
to the left, which is equivalent to
\text{tr}(\mathcal{F}^{-1}(U)\mathcal{F}(U^{*}))
. Therefore,

\displaystyle\text{tr}(Q_{n})=\text{tr}(UU^{*})=\text{tr}(\mathcal{F}^{-1}(U)\mathcal{F}(U^{*}))=\text{tr}(\beta^{-1}W^{*}\overline{\beta}^{-1}W)=\beta^{-1}\overline{\beta}^{-1}\text{tr}(W^{*}W)=\beta^{-1}\overline{\beta^{-1}}\text{tr}(Q_{n}^{\prime})

By relation (i), we get that
\text{tr}(Q_{n}^{\prime})=1=\text{tr}(Q_{n})
, and thus
\beta^{-1}\overline{\beta}^{-1}=1
. Hence,
\beta^{-1}=\overline{\beta}
. By instead taking trace of
U^{*}U
, we can do the same process as before and get
\overline{\alpha}=\alpha^{-1}
. Now we can see that
VV^{*}=WW^{*}=P_{n}^{\prime}
and
V^{*}V=W^{*}W=Q_{n}^{\prime}
giving that relation (iv) is satisfied for
V
and
V^{*}
as well.

Finally, we prove relation (v). Using the equalities found earlier we can see that

\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(U)

\displaystyle=\alpha W^{*}=\alpha\beta\beta^{-1}W^{*}=\alpha\beta V^{*}=\sigma_{n}V^{*},\text{ and}

\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(U^{*})

\displaystyle=\overline{\beta}^{-1}W=\beta W=V

which give the first equalities of each of the equations in relation (v). Further,

\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(V)

\displaystyle=\beta\mathcal{F}(W)=\beta\overline{\alpha}^{-1}U^{*}=\beta\alpha U^{*}=\sigma_{n}U^{*},\text{ and}

\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(V^{*})

\displaystyle=\beta^{-1}\mathcal{F}(W^{*})=\beta^{-1}\beta U=U

Taking
\mathcal{F}^{-1}
of these last two equalities we get
V=\sigma_{n}\mathcal{F}^{-1}(U^{*})
and
V^{*}=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(U)
. This completes showing relation (vi) and hence the entire theorem. ∎

Remark 3.1
.

We can always color a strand in its entirety by red or blue. Suppose a strand is colored more than one color. Then look at where the colors switch. If the switch is between red and blue then use color disagreement to make the diagram 0. If the switch is between black and red (or blue) then multiplying

by

In Theorem
4.11
we will prove that the elements
P_{1}
,
Q_{1}
,
U
,
U^{*}
,
V
, and
V^{*}
actually generate the planar algebra
\mathcal{P}
. Next, we will know show that if we have these elements as generators and the relations from Theorem
3.10
, we obtain the planar algebra
\mathcal{P}
.

4
Sufficient Relations for Affine
A
Finite Subfactor Planar Algebras

Theorem 4.1
.

(Sufficient relations for
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
)
Fix
n\in\mathbb{N}
and an
n
th root of unity
\sigma_{n}
. Let
\mathcal{P}
be the planar algebra with generators
P_{1}
,
Q_{1}
,
U
,
U^{*}
,
V
,
V^{*}
from Definition
3.1

with relations (i) through (vi) given in Definition
3.2
. Define
P_{1}
and
Q_{1}
to be self-adjoint,
U^{*}
to be the adjoint of
U
, and
V^{*}
to be the adjoint of
V
, then extend the * operation anti-linearly and on diagrams. Then
\mathcal{P}
is a subfactor planar algebra whose principal graph and dual principal graph are the
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
Dynkin diagrams given in Theorem
3.10
.

Throughout the rest of this section,
\mathcal{P}
will refer to the planar algebra defined through generators and relations given in the previous theorem. Fix
n\in\mathbb{N}
and a root of unity
\sigma_{n}
. Before proving Theorem
4.1
, we will prove a collection of facts following from this generators and relations presentation. It is clear that for any diagram
T
,
T^{*}
is obtained by vertical flipping and taking adjoints of boxes.

Lemma 4.2
.

The adjoint is well-defined.

Proof.

Relations (i), (ii), (iii), and (iv) satisfy that taking their adjoint gives the same equality back clearly. For relation (v), taking the adjoint of the
UU^{*}
equality gives the
U^{*}U
equality and vice versa, taking the adjoint of
VV^{*}
gives
V^{*}V
and vice versa. Finally, for relation (vi), taking the adjoint of the first equality,
\mathcal{F}(U)=\sigma_{n}V^{*}=\sigma_{n}\mathcal{F}^{-1}(U)
, gives
\mathcal{F}^{-1}(U^{*})=\sigma_{n}^{-1}V=\sigma_{n}^{-1}\mathcal{F}(U^{*})
. Multiplying this second set of equalities by a
\sigma_{n}
, we obtain the second set of equalities in relation (vi). Taking the adjoint again we will arrive at the first set of equalities. Therefore, the adjoint is well-defined. ∎

The next step in proving Theorem
4.1
is to show the the 0-box space,
\mathcal{P}_{0}
is one-dimensional. We do this in two parts. First, we show
\mathcal{P}_{0}
is at least one-dimensional by defining a surjection from
\mathcal{P}_{0}
to
\mathbb{C}
that sends
\emptyset_{+}
and
\emptyset_{-}
to 1. Then, to show that
\mathcal{P}_{0}
is at most one-dimensional, we give an evaluation algorithm for the 0-box space.

To define the function we use the fact that the strands in any diagram of a planar algebra partitions the square picture into regions. From this fact we state the following remark. This comes from the theory of van Kampen diagrams.

Remark 4.1
.

For any diagram in
\mathcal{P}
there exists a unique function from the regions of the diagram to the dihedral group
D_{n}=\langle r,b|r^{2}=b^{2}=(rb)^{n}=1\rangle
such that the region on the left-most boundary next to the star is assigned 1 and neighboring regions separated by a red (respectively blue) strand are assigned elements of the form
x
and
xr
(respectively
x
and
xb
).

We now define a surjection from
\mathcal{P}_{0}
to
\mathbb{C}
. Lemma
4.3
will show
f
is a well-defined surjection. It will then follow that
\mathcal{P}_{0}
is at least one-dimensional.

Define a function
f:\mathcal{P}_{0}\to\mathbb{C}
by the following. By strand decomposition and color disagreement it suffices to define
f
on diagrams where every strand is either red or blue in its entirety and then extend
f
linearly. Let
D\in\mathcal{P}_{0}
be such a diagram.

1.

If there are no
U,U^{*},V,
and
V^{*}
-boxes, define
f(D)=1
.

2.

If there is a
U
,
U^{*}
,
V
, or
V^{*}
box, enumerate them all. Say
U_{1},...,U_{a},U^{*}_{1},...,U^{*}_{b},V_{1},...,V_{c},V^{*}_{1},...,V^{*}_{d}
.

3.

Define a number,
\ell_{j}^{J}
, based on the following table where
w_{j}^{J}
is the element of
D
that corresponds to the region where
J_{j}
’s star lies.

When
J=U
or
V
,

When
J=U^{*}
or
V^{*}
,

\bullet
if
w_{j}^{J}=(rb)^{m}
, then
\ell_{j}^{J}=m
,

\bullet
if
w_{j}^{J}=(rb)^{m}
, then
\ell_{j}^{J}=-m
,

\bullet
if
w_{j}^{J}=b(rb)^{m}
, then
\ell_{j}^{J}=m+1
,

\bullet
if
w_{j}^{J}=b(rb)^{m}
, then
\ell_{j}^{J}=-(m+1)

\bullet
if
w_{j}^{J}=(br)^{m}
, then
\ell_{j}^{J}=-m
, and

\bullet
if
w_{j}^{J}=(br)^{m}
, then
\ell_{j}^{J}=m
, and

\bullet
if
w_{j}^{J}=r(br)^{m}
, then
\ell_{j}^{J}=-m
.

\bullet
if
w_{j}^{J}=r(br)^{m}
, then
\ell_{j}^{J}=m
.

4.

Define
\ell^{D}=\left(\sum_{j=1}^{a}\ell_{j}^{U}+\sum_{j=1}^{b}\ell_{j}^{U^{*}}\right)+\left(\sum_{j=1}^{c}\ell_{j}^{V}+\sum_{j=1}^{d}\ell_{j}^{V^{*}}\right)\text{ }(\text{mod }n)

5.

Define
f(D)=\sigma^{\ell^{D}}

6.

Extend
f
linearly to evaluate on all of
\mathcal{P}_{0}
.

There are some things to immediately note about this function that will be said without proof.

Remark 4.2
.

The number of
U
and
U^{*}
boxes, as well as the number of
V
and
V^{*}
boxes, are equal. That is
a=b
and
c=d
.

Remark 4.3
.

The table in step 4 gives a well-defined function from
D_{n}
to the integers.

Lemma 4.3
.

f
is a well-defined surjection.

Proof.

To show that
f
is well-defined we must show that
f
is invariant under the relations of
\mathcal{P}
.

f
is obviously invariant under the strand decomposition and color disagreements.

If
D
and
D^{\prime}
are identical except in a local region where
D
looks like the left-hand side of a saddle relation and
D^{\prime}
has the right-hand side of the saddle relation, then its clear that the labellings of the regions by elements of
D_{n}
will be identical. The same is true for the bubble relations. Thus
f
is invariant under these two relations.

Let
D
and
D^{\prime}
are identical except in a local region
D
is
UU^{*}
written as left-hand diagram in the unitary relations and
D^{\prime}
is the right-hand diagram with no boxes. First notice that the stars of
U
and
U^{*}
lie in the same region. Their associated
\ell
-values will cancel. What’s left to check is that the regions outside of this local neighborhood are identically labelled. Any regions to the top and bottom of this local region will be labelled the same since the top and bottom boundary data is the same for both
D
and
D^{\prime}
, so
f
is invariant under this relation. Similar arguments can be made for the rest of the unitary relations.

For the final relation, let
D
,
D^{\prime}
, and
D^{\prime\prime}
be diagrams in
\mathcal{P}_{0}
, identical except in a local region
D
looks like the left hand side of the first click relation
\mathcal{F}(U)
,
D^{\prime}
looks like
V^{*}
, and
D^{\prime\prime}
is
\mathcal{F}^{-1}(U)
. Again, we need to check that the regions outside this neighborhood are labelled the same as well as that the
\ell
-values coming from these boxes are the same for
D^{\prime}
and
D^{\prime\prime}
and are one less than
D
.

The former statement is clear. The strands on the top and bottom of the diagrams are the same colors in all 3 neighborhoods. The right-most region will then also be the same label.

Now consider the latter statement. Let
x
be the group element in the left-most region of the local neighborhood. We break this into cases.

If
x=(rb)^{m}
, then for
D
,
xb=r(br)^{(m-1)}
Therefore, the
\ell
-value of
U
in
D
be
-m+1
. For
D^{\prime}
,
x=(rb)^{m}
is the group element labelled the region of
V^{*}
’s star, so the
\ell
-value for
V^{*}
will be
-m
. For
D^{\prime}
,
xr=r(br)^{m}
, which will give
U
and
\ell
-value of
-m
.

If
x=b(rb)^{m}
, then for
D
,
xb=b(rb)^{m}b=(br)^{m}
, and the
\ell
-value for
U
will be
-m
. For
D^{\prime}
,
V^{*}
’s
\ell
-value is
-m-1
. For
D^{\prime\prime}
,
xr=(br)^{m+1}
, so
U
has an
\ell
-value of
-m-1
.

If
x=(br)^{m}
, then for
D
,
xb=b(rb)^{m}
, giving
U
an
\ell
-value of
m+1
. For
D^{\prime}
,
V^{*}
has an
\ell
-value of
m
. For
D^{\prime\prime}
,
xr=b(rb)^{m-1}
, which gives
U
an
\ell
-value of
m
.

If
x=r(br)^{m}
, then for
D
, the region of
U
’s star is labelled
xb=(rb)^{m+1}
, which gives
U
an
\ell
-value of
m+1
. For
D^{\prime}
, the
\ell
-value of
V^{*}
is
m
. For
D^{\prime\prime}
, region of
U
’s star is labelled
xr=(rb)^{m}
, which gives
U
and
\ell
-value of
m
.

Thus, in all these cases, when multiplying the
D^{\prime}
and
D^{\prime\prime}
by another value of
\sigma_{n}
, the resulting values of the function for
D
,
D^{\prime}
, and
D^{\prime\prime}
will be identical. A similar computation can be done for the second click relation.

Therefore
f
is invariant under the relations of
\mathcal{P}
and is well-defined. ∎

Corollary 4.4
.

\mathcal{P}_{0}
is at least one-dimensional.

Proof.

f
is a well-defined function. Further,
f(\emptyset_{+})=1
, so
f
is a surjection. Therefore
\mathcal{P}_{0}
is at least one-dimensional. ∎

Next, we define an algorithm to evaluate any element in
\mathcal{P}_{0}
. In doing so, we show that
\mathcal{P}_{0}
is at most one-dimensional.

Evaluation Algorithm for
\mathcal{P}_{0}
:

By strand decomposition and color disagreement it suffices to define the algorithm on diagrams where every strand is either red or blue in its entirety then extend linearly. Let
D\in\mathcal{P}_{0}
be such a diagram.

1.

If
D
has no
U
,
U^{*}
,
V
, and
V^{*}
boxes, skip to step 10.

2.

If there is a
U
,
U^{*}
,
V
, or
V^{*}
-box, pick one of them and label it
W_{\text{up}}
.

3.

Due to the checkerboard shading and the alternating colors of the strands, the strands of
W_{\text{up}}
cannot have both its end on itself. Since
D
is in the 0-box space, all the strands of
D
cannot go to the boundary, so for the left-most strand of the bottom of
W_{\text{up}}
must lie on another box. Label this box
W_{\text{down}}
.

4.

Click
W_{\text{down}}
so that the connected strand is the top leftmost strand. This may multiply the diagram by some factor of
\sigma_{n}
as well as change the type of box. We will continue to call this box
W_{\text{down}}
.

5.

Isotope
W_{\text{down}}
so that is is directly below
W_{\text{up}}
.

6.

The strands adjacent to the connected strands of
W_{\text{up}}
and
W_{\text{down}}
must be of the same color as well as agree with shading. The strand adjacent on the right of the connected strand of
W_{\text{down}}
must be able to be isotoped so that with the strand right of the connected strand of
W_{\text{up}}
, the saddle relation can be performed so that the ends of one of the strands lies on both
W_{\text{up}}
and
W_{\text{down}}
.

7.

Inductively repeat the process of connecting the strands adjacent on the right of the previous strand of
W_{\text{up}}
until
W_{\text{up}}
and
W_{\text{down}}
are connected by
n
adjacent strands.

8.

The bottom
n
strands of
W_{\text{up}}
are now connected to the top
n
strands of
W_{\text{down}}
so
W_{\text{up}}
and
W_{\text{down}}
must be adjoints of each other. Therefore we can use the unitary relations to rewrite
D
as a diagram with two less boxes. Repeat steps 2-7 until we are left with 0 or 1 boxes.

9.

If 1 box remains, its strands must connect to itself, so
D=0
.

10.

If 0 boxes remain,
D
is now a closed diagram consisting of only red or blue strands and is maybe multiplied by a scalar. Starting with the innermost loop, repeatedly pop the loops using the bubble relations.
D
will then evaluate to a multiple of
\emptyset_{+}
or
\emptyset_{-}
.

With the evaluation algorithm defined, now the following lemma and its corollary becomes instant.

Lemma 4.5
.

\mathcal{P}_{0}
is at most one-dimensional.

Corollary 4.6
.

\mathcal{P}_{0}
is one-dimensional.

Lemma 4.7
.

All of the diagrams in the saddle relations:

(i)

P_{1}\otimes P^{\prime}_{1}
,

(ii)

Q_{1}\otimes Q^{\prime}_{1}
,

(iii)

P^{\prime}_{1}\otimes P_{1}
, and

(iv)

Q^{\prime}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}
.

are minimal projections. Further, (i) and (ii) are isomorphic to
\emptyset_{+}
and (iii) and (iv) are isomorphic to
\emptyset_{-}
.

Proof.

We will just show
P_{1}\otimes P_{1}^{\prime}
is a minimal projection. The rest of the items have nearly identical arguments. It is clear that
P_{1}\otimes P_{1}^{\prime}
is a projection. Let
f\in\text{Hom}(P_{1}\otimes P_{1}^{\prime},P_{1}\otimes P_{1}^{\prime})
. If
f\neq 0
, then using the evaluation algorithm to reduce the number of boxes in
f
connected by a strand we can assume
f
can be written to be a collection of boxes not connected to any other box and has no closed components. Thus the strands of all the boxes in
f
must go to the top and bottom of the diagram, as
f\neq 0
. However, there are only red strands on the boundary and all boxes for have at least one blue strand. Thus
f
cannot contain a box.

Assume
f
has no boxes. Then it is clear the only options for
f
are scalar multiples of
P_{1}\otimes P_{1}^{\prime}
or scalar multiples of the cup/cap diagram on the left side of the saddle relation. Both of these will result in
f
being a scalar multiple of itself, due to the saddle relations. Therefore the dimension of
\text{Hom}(P_{1}\otimes P_{1}^{\prime},P_{1}\otimes P_{1}^{\prime})
is at most 1. Since the trace of
P_{1}\otimes P_{1}^{\prime}
is 1, we get that the dimension of
\text{Hom}(P_{1}\otimes P_{1}^{\prime},P_{1}\otimes P_{1}^{\prime})
is 1, so
P_{1}\otimes P_{1}^{\prime}
is a minimal projection.

We want to show that
\emptyset_{+}\cong P_{1}\otimes P_{1}^{\prime}\cong Q_{1}\otimes Q_{1}^{\prime}
and
\emptyset_{-}\cong P_{1}^{\prime}\otimes P_{1}\cong Q_{1}^{\prime}\otimes Q_{1}
. Since the dimension of
\mathcal{P}_{0,\pm}
is 1, we know that both
\emptyset_{+}
and
\emptyset_{-}
are minimal projections. By the saddle relations,
P_{1}\otimes P_{1}^{\prime}
,
P_{1}^{\prime}\otimes P_{1}
,
Q_{1}\otimes Q_{1}^{\prime}
, and
Q_{1}^{\prime}\otimes Q_{1}
are all factoring through either
\emptyset_{+}
or
\emptyset_{-}
. Since all of these diagrams are nonzero, this gives the desired isomorphisms. ∎

Next we show that the
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
Dynkin diagram are the correct principal and dual principal graphs for this planar algebra.

Lemma 4.8
.

The principal graphs of
\mathcal{P}_{0}
are the graphs given in (
12
) for
n\geq 2
and (
13
) for
n=1
.

Proof.

Define
P_{k}=P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes\overset{(k-1)}{...}\otimes R_{1}
,
P_{k}^{\prime}=\overline{P}_{1}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes\overset{(k-1)}{...}\otimes\overline{R}_{1}
,
Q_{\ell}=Q_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\otimes\overset{(\ell-1)}{...}\otimes\overline{R}_{2}
, and
Q_{\ell}^{\prime}=\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes P_{1}\otimes\overset{(\ell-1)}{...}\otimes R_{2}
for
1\leq k\leq n
and
1\leq\ell\leq n-1
, where
R_{1},R_{2}\in\{P_{1},\overline{Q}_{1}\}
and depend on
n
. Additionally, define
P_{0}=\emptyset_{+}
and
P^{\prime}_{0}=\emptyset_{-}
, which were already shown to be minimal projections since
\mathcal{P}_{0,\pm}
is one-dimensional. As the adjoint distributes over
\otimes
and
P_{1}
,
P_{1}^{\prime}=\overline{P}_{1}
,
Q_{1}
, and
Q_{1}^{\prime}=\overline{Q}_{1}
are clearly projections, for all
1\leq k\leq n
and
1\leq\ell\leq n-1

P_{k}
,
P_{k}^{\prime}
,
Q_{\ell}
, and
Q_{\ell}^{\prime}
are projections.

To then show that these are in fact minimal projections, we want to show that for all
1\leq k\leq n
,
1\leq\ell\leq n-1
, the dimensions of
\text{Hom}(P_{k},P_{k})
,
\text{Hom}(P_{k}^{\prime},P_{k}^{\prime})
,
\text{Hom}(Q_{\ell},Q_{\ell})
, and
\text{Hom}(Q_{\ell}^{\prime},Q_{\ell}^{\prime})
are 1. Notice that taking the trace of all these projections gives 1, so the dimension of these hom-spaces is greater than 0. We will just prove the dimension of the hom-space of
P_{k}
is 1. The rest of the dimensions can be found nearly identically.

Fix
k
and some
f\in\text{Hom}(P_{k},P_{k})
. Diagrammatically we have

\displaystyle f=\hbox to56.14pt{\vbox to60.55pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 7.34547pt\lower-20.31683pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
