If
f
has two
U
,
U^{*}
,
V
, and
V^{*}
boxes connected by a strand, we can use the method outlined in the evaluation algorithm for
\mathcal{P}_{0}
to write
f
with two less boxes. Thus it is sufficient to think of
f
as either having zero boxes, or having a collection of boxes each not connected to each other. In the latter case, this means all the strands of these boxes must be connected to the boundary or themselves. If
k<n
, then the number of points on the boundary of the
f
-box is less than
2n
, so all the boxes inside of
f
would have to have some strands connecting to themselves, which would make
f=0
. If
k=n
then the number of points on the boundary of the
f
-box is
2n
. If there is more than one box inside of
f
then one of the boxes must have at least one strand connecting to itself, making
f=0
. If
f
has exactly one box, then since the strands of any box alternates in color and the top and bottom leftmost strand on the boundary of
f
are both red, for all the strands of the box to connect to the boundary of
f
would require some color disagreement, making
f=0
.
Therefore, for
f
to be nonzero,
f
must have zero
U
,
U^{*}
,
V
, and
V^{*}
boxes.

Assume
f\neq 0
, which by the preceding paragraph means that
f
has zero boxes. The strands on the boundary of
f
are alternating in color on the top and on the bottom, so
f
cannot have any caps or cups. Therefore,
f
must be some straight strands along with some circles, which can be popped for a scalar, say
\lambda\in\mathbb{C}
. The only possibility for
f\neq 0
with straight strands would mean the straight strands are
P_{k}
. Therefore
f=\lambda P_{k}
, giving that the dimension of
\text{Hom}(P_{k},P_{k})
is 1.

Next we show that these are nonisomorphic minimal projections by showing that there are no nonzero morphisms between any of these distinct projections. We break this into cases depending on if the projections start with the same color strand. Define
P_{0}=Q_{0}=\emptyset_{+}
and
P^{\prime}_{0}=Q^{\prime}_{0}=\emptyset_{-}
. Fix
0\leq k\leq n
and
0\leq\ell\leq n-1
.

Case 1:
Suppose that
f
is a nonzero morphism between the
P_{k}
or
P_{k}^{\prime}
projection and the
Q_{\ell}
or
Q_{\ell}^{\prime}
projection. Notice that on the boundary of
f
, the top and bottom leftmost strands will be of different colors. Without loss of generality, assume that
f
has no closed component. Using the method outline in the evaluation algorithm for
\mathcal{P}_{0}
, write
f
as a diagram where all of the boxes are not connected to each other. If the strands of the boxes are connected to themselves, then
f=0
. So every boxes’ strands must connect to the boundary as
f\neq 0
. The number of strands on the boundary is
k+\ell
. If
k+\ell<2n
then there are not enough points on the boundary for even one box. As
f\neq 0
, we then know
f
contains no boxes. If
k+\ell=2n
then
k=\ell=n
. However,
\ell\leq n-1
, so this case is eliminated. Now we are left with considering
f
with no boxes inside. However, since the leftmost stands are of opposite colors and the colors on the top and bottom alternate, there is no such nonzero diagram
f
.

Case 2:
Suppose that
f
is a nonzero morphism between two minimal projections starting with the same color on the leftside. Without loss of generality, lets assume
f
is a morphism from
P_{k_{1}}
to
P_{k_{2}}
where
k_{1},k_{2}\in\{0,...,n\}
. Again, we only need to consider the case where
f
has no closed component and all of the strands of the boxes connect to the boundary. The number of strands on the boundary is
k_{1}+k_{2}
which is strictly less than
2n
unless
k_{1}=k_{2}
which would imply the projections are equal. Thus all that is left to consider when
f
has no boxes. There can be no caps or cups in
f
due to the alternating colors of the strands. Therefore, the only options is for
f
to be alternating strands and again
k_{1}=k_{2}
.

Naturally define
Q_{n}
and
Q_{n}^{\prime}
. Using the same methods as before we can show
Q_{n}
and
Q_{n}^{\prime}
are minimal projection nonisomorphic to
P_{k}
,
P_{k}^{\prime}
,
Q_{\ell}
, and
Q_{\ell}^{\prime}
for
0\leq k,\ell\leq n-1
. However, it is true that
Q_{n}\cong P_{n}
and
Q_{n}^{\prime}\cong P_{n}^{\prime}
. To see this, notice that
U
and
V
are morphisms between
Q_{n}
and
P_{n}
and
Q_{n}^{\prime}
and
P_{n}^{\prime}
respectively. Since the trace of
UU^{*}
and
VV^{*}
are both nonzero,
U
and
V
are nonzero morphisms. Therefore there’s a nonzero morphism between minimal projections giving that
Q_{n}\cong P_{n}
and
Q_{n}^{\prime}\cong P_{n}^{\prime}
, as desired.

What is left to show is that these nonisomorphic minimal projections satisfy the fusion rules for the
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
Dynkin diagram with labellings given by (
5
) or (
6
). First, let
n\geq 2
and define
Q_{n}=Q_{n-1}\otimes\overline{R}_{3}
where
\overline{R}_{3}\neq\overline{R}_{2}
and
R_{3}\in\{P_{1},\overline{Q}_{1}\}
, and define
Q_{n}^{\prime}
similarly. Using the strand decompositions,
\emptyset_{+}\otimes X\cong P_{1}\oplus Q_{1}
and
\emptyset_{-}\otimes Y\cong\overline{P}_{1}\oplus\overline{Q}_{1}
. Now we will show inductively that
P_{k}\otimes R
(where
R
is
Y
when
k
is odd and
X
when
k
is even) is isomorphic to
P_{k-1}\oplus P_{k+1}
for
1\leq k\leq n-1
. Similar arguments will then show the necessary tensor decompositions for
P_{k}^{\prime}
,
Q_{k}
, and
Q_{k}^{\prime}
.

For the base case, notice that
P_{1}\otimes Y\cong P_{1}\otimes(P_{1}^{\prime}\oplus Q_{1}^{\prime})\cong(P_{1}\otimes P_{1}^{\prime})\oplus(P_{1}\otimes Q_{1}^{\prime})\cong\emptyset_{+}\oplus P_{2}
using strand decomposition and Lemma
4.7
. Next assume
P_{k}\otimes R\cong P_{k-1}\oplus P_{k+1}
up to some
k<n-1
. Then if
n-1
is even,

\displaystyle P_{n-1}\otimes X\cong P_{n-1}\otimes(P_{1}+Q_{1})\cong(P_{n-1}\otimes P_{1})\oplus(P_{n-1}\otimes Q_{1})

When
n-1
is even, the rightmost strand of
P_{n-1}
will be
\overline{Q}_{1}
. Therefore
P_{n-1}\otimes Q_{1}\cong P_{n-2}
and
P_{n-1}\otimes P_{1}\cong P_{n}
. Thus
P_{n-1}\otimes X\cong P_{n}\oplus P_{n-2}
. If
n-1
is odd,

\displaystyle P_{n-1}\otimes Y\cong P_{n-1}\otimes(\overline{P}_{1}+\overline{Q}_{1})\cong(P_{n-1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1})\oplus(P_{n-1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1})

When
n-1
is odd, the rightmost strand of
P_{n-1}
is
P_{1}
so
P_{n-1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\cong\emptyset_{+}
and
P_{n-1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\cong P_{n}
. Therefore
P_{n-1}\cong P_{n-2}\oplus P_{n}
, concluding our inductive proof.

Next I show that
P_{n}\otimes R\cong P_{n-1}\oplus Q_{n-1}
. Following the method of the above paragraph gives
P_{n}\otimes R\cong P_{n-1}\oplus(P_{n}\otimes S)
where
S=P_{1}
if
n
is even and
S=\overline{Q}_{1}
when
n
is odd. Further,
P_{n}\cong Q_{n}
, so
P_{n}\otimes S\cong Q_{n}\otimes S
which will be isomorphic to
Q_{n-1}\otimes\emptyset_{+}
or
Q_{n-1}\otimes\emptyset_{-}
depending on the parity of
n
. Therefore
P_{n}\otimes R\cong P_{n-1}\oplus Q_{n-1}
.

For
n=1
,
\emptyset_{+}\otimes X\cong X=P_{1}+Q_{1}
by definition of tensor and strand decomposition. Further, using that
P_{1}\cong Q_{1}
we get
X\cong P_{1}\oplus Q_{1}\cong P_{1}\oplus P_{1}
. Additionally,
P_{1}\otimes Y\cong P_{1}\otimes(\overline{P}_{1}+\overline{Q}_{1})
by the strand decomposition, which is isomorphic to
P_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}+P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\cong\emptyset_{+}\oplus\emptyset_{+}
by Lemma
4.7
.

Similarly, for any
n\in\mathbb{N}
, one can show the necessary tensor decompositions for the dual principal graph which concludes the lemma. ∎

Lemma 4.9
.

\mathcal{P}
is spherical.

Proof.

To show this lemma it suffices to prove that
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}=\text{ span}\{P_{1},Q_{1}\}
and
\mathcal{P}_{1,-}=\{\overline{P}_{1},\overline{Q}_{1}\}
. The inclusion of
\text{ span}\{P_{1},Q_{1}\}
into
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
is obvious. Let
T
be an element in
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
. Then
T
is a linear combination of diagrams from
\text{Hom}(P_{1},P_{1})
,
\text{Hom}(Q_{1},Q_{1})
,
\text{Hom}(P_{1},Q_{1})
, and
\text{Hom}(Q_{1},P_{1})
. Since
P_{1}
and
Q_{1}
are nonisomorphic minimal projections we get that the only hom-spaces with nonzero dimension are
\text{Hom}(P_{1},P_{1})
and
\text{Hom}(Q_{1},Q_{1})
. Further, these hom-spaces are both one-dimensional. Therefore
T
is in
\text{ span}\{P_{1},Q_{1}\}
, so
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}=\text{ span}\{P_{1},Q_{1}\}
. The proof of
\mathcal{P}_{1,-}
is the same. ∎

Lemma 4.10
.

\mathcal{P}
is positive definite.

Proof.

In
[
MPS10
]
the authors give and explicit positive definite basis of each of the box spaces for any planar algebra whose corresponding category of projections is semisimple. We can adapt this proof slightly to instead give a positive definite basis of
\mathcal{P}_{2m,\pm}
which is now identified with the hom-space from
\emptyset
to alternating tensor products of
X
and
\overline{X}
. The trees they create would also alternate on the boundary between
X
and
\overline{X}
. Additionally, in our case,
X
is not a minimal projection, however, they do not need this in their proof. The authors then show in Theorem 4.18 that their defined tree diagrams with boundary labelled entirely by
X
give a positive orthogonal basis for the space
\text{Hom}(\emptyset,X^{\otimes k})
, which corresponds to our vector spaces
\mathcal{P}_{2m,\pm}
. The only thing left to check is that all of the minimal projections have positive trace. Indeed,
\text{tr}(P_{1})=\text{tr}(Q_{1})=\text{tr}(\overline{P}_{1})=\text{tr}(\overline{Q}_{1})=1
and the rest of the minimal projections are tensor products of these elements, so the minimal projections all have trace 1, so
\mathcal{P}
is positive definite. ∎

Proof of Theorem
4.1
.

All of the work has already been done. From Lemma
4.5
we get that the space of closed diagrams is one-dimensional. Lemma
4.9
gives that
\mathcal{P}
is spherical and Lemma
4.8
gives that the principal graph is the
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
Dynkin diagram as shown in Lemma
4.8
. Finally, we get that
\mathcal{P}
is positive definite from Lemma
4.10
, which completes the proof. ∎

Now we can return to Theorem
3.10
and show that the elements listed are in fact generators so the Theorem is a presentation of the planar algebra.

Theorem 4.11
.

The elements
P_{1},Q_{1},U,U^{*},V,
and
V^{*}
from Theorem
3.10
generate
\mathcal{P}
.

Proof.

From Theorem
4.1
, we know
P_{1},Q_{1},U,U^{*},V
, and
V^{*}
generate
\mathcal{P}
, a subfactor planar algebra with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
. Let
\mathcal{Q}
be the subfactor planar algebra from Theorem
3.10
. The elements
P_{1},Q_{1},U,U^{*},V
, and
V^{*}
will generate
\mathcal{Q}
if for all
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
,
\text{dim}(\mathcal{P}_{k,\pm})=\text{dim}(\mathcal{Q}_{k,\pm})
. Returning to the explicit positive definite basis for each of the box spaces created in
[
MPS10
]
, these bases rely solely on the principal graph and the traces of the minimal projections. As these are equal in both
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{Q}
, we get that
\text{dim}(\mathcal{P}_{k,\pm})=\text{dim}(\mathcal{Q}_{k,\pm})
for all
k\geq 0
. Thus
P_{1}
,
Q_{1}
,
U
,
U^{*}
,
V
, and
V^{*}
are generators of
\mathcal{Q}
since they are generators of
\mathcal{P}
. ∎

5
Distinctness and Fulfillment of Presentations for Affine
A
Finite Subfactor Planar Algebras

From the Theorems
4.1
and
4.11
we find that Theorem
3.10
with generators
P_{1},Q_{1},U,U^{*},V,
and
V^{*}
give
n
presentations of the subfactor planar algebra with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
. It is then quite natural to ask if any of these are isomorphic and if there are any presentations left to be found. Indeed, none of these are isomorphic and there are no more, so we can prove the below theorem, which is a known result by Popa
[
Pop94
]
; however, our proof is strictly using the planar algebra presentations.

Theorem 5.1
.

There are exactly
n
nonisomorphic subfactor planar algebras with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
.

First we will prove that none of the
n
presentations given are isomorphic.

Lemma 5.2
.

Let
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{Q}
be planar algebras given by generators from Definition
3.1
and relations from Definition
3.2
, using
n
th roots of unity
\sigma
and
\tilde{\sigma}
respectively. If
\sigma\neq\tilde{\sigma}
then
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{Q}
are nonisomorphic.

Proof.

When
n=1
there is only one 1th root of unity, so we can assume
n\geq 2
. Call the boxes of
\mathcal{P}
:
U
,
U^{*}
,
V
, and
V^{*}
and the boxes of
\mathcal{Q}
:
\tilde{U}
,
\tilde{U}^{*}
,
\tilde{V}
, and
\tilde{V}^{*}
. Call the distinct minimal projections in
\mathcal{P}_{1,+}
and
\mathcal{Q}_{1,+}

P_{1}
,
Q_{1}
,
\tilde{P}_{1}
, and
\tilde{Q}_{1}
respectively. For sake of contradiction let
\theta:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{Q}
be a planar algebra isomorphism. Then
\theta_{1,+}:\mathcal{P}_{1,+}\to\mathcal{Q}_{1,+}
is a bijective map.

A planar algebra isomorphism must preserve minimal projections so either
\theta_{1,+}(P_{1})=\tilde{P}_{1}
and
\theta_{1,+}(Q_{1})=\tilde{Q}_{1}
or
\theta_{1,+}(P_{1})=\tilde{Q}_{1}
and
\theta_{1,+}(Q_{1})=\tilde{P}_{1}
. From knowing
\theta_{1,+}
, we can completely determine
\theta_{1,-}
. Let
T
be the 1-click tangle on the
(1,+)
-box space. Then
\theta_{1,-}(Z_{T}(P_{1}))=\theta_{1,-}(\overline{P}_{1})

which is equivalent to
Z_{T}\left(\theta_{1,+}(P_{1})\right)
.

A planar algebra isomorphism also preserves tensor product. Consider when
\theta_{1,+}(P_{1})=\tilde{P}_{1}
. Since
\text{Hom}(P_{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{1}\otimes\overset{(n-1)}{...}\otimes R_{1},Q_{1}\otimes\overline{P}_{1}\otimes\overset{(n-1)}{...}\otimes R_{1})
is one-dimensional, there exists a
\rho_{1}\in\mathbb{C}
such that
\theta(U^{*})=\rho_{1}\tilde{U}^{*}
and similarly, there is a
\rho_{2}\in\mathbb{C}
with
\theta(V)=\rho_{2}\tilde{V}
. By definition of isomorphism,
\mathcal{F}(\theta(U^{*}))=\mathcal{F}(\rho_{1}\tilde{U}^{*})=\rho_{1}\mathcal{F}(\tilde{U}^{*})=\rho_{1}\tilde{V}
is equivalent to
\theta(\mathcal{F}(U^{*}))=\theta(V)=\rho_{2}\tilde{V}
giving that
\rho_{1}=\rho_{2}
. Since
\theta
is an isomorphism and
U^{*}
is a generator of a one-dimensional hom-space,
\rho_{1}\neq 0
. Again, using the definition of isomorphism,
\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\theta(U^{*}))=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\rho_{1}\tilde{U}^{*})=\rho_{1}\tilde{\sigma}^{-1}\tilde{V}
is equivalent to
\theta(\mathcal{F}^{-1}(U^{*}))=\sigma^{-1}\theta(V)=\sigma^{-1}\rho_{1}\tilde{V}
. Therefore,
\tilde{\sigma}^{-1}=\sigma^{-1}
, which is a contradiction.

Consider when
\theta_{1,+}(P_{1})=\tilde{Q}_{1}
. Similar to case (ii), there exists
\rho_{1},\rho_{2},\rho_{3},
and
\rho_{4}\in\mathbb{C}-\{0\}
where
\theta(U)=\rho_{1}\tilde{U}^{*}
,
\theta(V^{*})=\rho_{2}\tilde{V}
,
\theta(U^{*})=\rho_{3}\tilde{U}
, and
\theta(V)=\rho_{4}\tilde{V}^{*}
. Using the click relations we get
\theta(\mathcal{F}(U))=\theta(\sigma V^{*})=\sigma\rho_{2}\tilde{V}
is equivalent to
\mathcal{F}(\theta(U))=\mathcal{F}(\rho_{1}\tilde{U}^{*})=\rho_{1}\tilde{V}
, so
\sigma=\rho_{1}/\rho_{2}
. However,
\theta(\mathcal{F}(V^{*}))=\theta(U)=\rho_{1}\tilde{U}^{*}
equals
\mathcal{F}(\theta(V^{*}))=\mathcal{F}(\rho_{2}\tilde{V})=\rho_{2}\tilde{\sigma}\tilde{U}^{*}
so
\tilde{\sigma}=\rho_{1}/\rho_{2}
, implying that
\tilde{\sigma}=\sigma
. Therefore if
\sigma\neq\tilde{\sigma}
,
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{Q}
are nonisomorphic. ∎

Proof of Theorem
5.1
.

By Lemma
5.2
, none of the
n
presentations found are isomorphic. Thus we have at least
n
nonisomorphic subfactor planar algebras with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
. By Theorems
3.10
and
4.11
if we have a subfactor planar algebra with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
then it must have one of the presentations listed. Thus there are exactly
n
nonisomorphic subfactor planar algerbas with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
. ∎

6
Necessary Relations for Affine
A
Finite Unshaded Planar Algebras

While the affine
A
principal graphs for subfactor planar algebras must have an even number of vertices on their principal graph, we will see in this section that there is no such requirement for unshaded subfactor planar algebras. However, we will also see that depending on the parity of the number of vertices, the number of nonisomorphic planar algebras will vary. Fix
n\in\mathbb{N}
and define
\mathcal{P}
to be a unshaded subfactor planar algebra with principal graph the
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
Dynkin diagram and let
\mathcal{P^{\prime}}
be a unshaded subfactor planar algebra with principal graph the
\tilde{A}_{2n}
Dynkin diagram. The next goal is to find all diagrammatic presentations of these planar algebras. We find that many of these results have similar proofs to the shaded case and thus will omit repetitive proofs as well as omit proofs for
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
that are essentially the same as
\mathcal{P}
. Define

\displaystyle X=\text{ }\hbox to0.8pt{\vbox to20.72pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.4pt\lower-0.4pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{}}{}

By Lemma
3.1
we already know
\mathcal{P}
has index 4. The same proof shows that
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
has index 4.

Vertices of a principal graph of an unshaded subfactor planar algebra

have the principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
with the following labelling when

[\emptyset]

(14)

and when

,

[\emptyset]

[P_{1}]

(15)

and let

have principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n}
with the following labelling

[\emptyset]
[P_{1}]
[Q_{1}]
[P_{2}]
[Q_{2}]
[P_{n-1}]
[Q_{n-1}]
[P_{n}]
[Q_{n}]
…

(16)

where each
P_{i}
,
1\leq i\leq n
, and
Q_{j}
,
1\leq j\leq n
, are representatives of their respective equivalence class. It should be clear from context if we are referring to the projections in
\mathcal{P}
or
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
.

By Lemma
3.1
, the trace of all the minimal projections are 1 in
\mathcal{P}
(and
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
) and by Lemma
3.2
, for all but those with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{1}
, there is a unique representative of
[P_{1}]
and
[Q_{1}]
in
\mathcal{P}_{1}
(respectively
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{1})
, which we will call
P_{1}
and
Q_{1}
and
X=P_{1}+Q_{1}
. Further, Lemma
3.4
gives that
\{P_{1},Q_{1}\}
form a basis of
\mathcal{P}_{1}
(respectively
\mathcal{P}_{1}^{\prime}
) for all but the planar algebras with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{1}
.

Lemma 6.1
.

For all unshaded subfactor planar algebras with affine
A
principal graphs, except
\tilde{A}_{1}
, the distinct minimal projections in the 1-box space,
P_{1}
and
Q_{1}
satisfy that either they are self-dual or are dual to each other.

Proof.

Without loss of generality, consider
\mathcal{P}
. Since
\{P_{1},Q_{1}\}
form a basis of
\mathcal{P}_{1}
, there exists
\lambda,\mu,\nu,\xi\in\mathbb{C}
so that
\overline{P}_{1}=\lambda P_{1}+\mu Q_{1}
and
\overline{Q}_{1}=\nu P_{1}+\xi Q_{1}
. Using that
P_{1}^{2}=P_{1}
,
Q_{1}^{2}=Q_{1}
,
P_{1}Q_{1}=Q_{1}P_{1}=0
, and that these properties must hold for their duals, we get that
\overline{P}_{1}
and
\overline{Q}_{1}
are distinct minimal projections in the 1-box space. Thus either
\overline{P}_{1}=P_{1}
and
\overline{Q}_{1}=Q_{1}
or
\overline{P}_{1}=Q_{1}
and
\overline{Q}_{1}=P_{1}
. ∎

Lemma 6.2
.

For unshaded subfactor planar algebras with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{1}
, there exists
R_{1},Q_{1}\in\mathcal{P}_{1}
isomorphic to
P_{1}
with
R_{1}Q_{1}=Q_{1}R_{1}=0
and
X=R_{1}+Q_{1}
, where either
R_{1}
and
Q_{1}
are self-dual or dual to each other.

Proof.

From the principal graph,
X\cong P_{1}\oplus P_{1}
which gives that the dimension of
\mathcal{P}_{1}
is 4. Further,
\mathcal{P}_{1}
is an associative algebra isomorphic to
\text{Hom}(P_{1}\oplus P_{1},P_{1}\oplus P_{1})
. As
P_{1}
is minimal projection, this hom-space is isomorphic to
M_{2}(\mathbb{C})
. The dual map of is an anti-involution of
\mathcal{P}
. For any anti-involution of
M_{2}(\mathbb{C})
, there exists nonzero
R_{1},Q_{1}
in
M_{2}(\mathbb{C})
that are either fixed or swapped such that
R_{1}^{2}=R_{1}
,
Q_{1}^{2}=Q_{1}
,
R_{1}+Q_{1}=I
, and
R_{1}Q_{1}=Q_{1}R_{1}=0
. As
\mathcal{P}_{1}
is isomorphic to
M_{2}(\mathbb{C})
this implies that there exists elements in
\mathcal{P}_{1}
, abusing notation we will still call them
R_{1}
and
Q_{1}
, such that
X\cong R_{1}\oplus Q_{1}
,
R_{1}Q_{1}=Q_{1}R_{1}=0
,
R_{1}^{2}=R_{1}
,
Q_{1}^{2}=Q_{1}
. ∎

When
n=1
let
P_{1}
and
Q_{1}
refer to the elements
R_{1}
and
Q_{1}
in the previous , respectively.

For our diagrammatic descriptions of unshaded subfactor planar algebras with principal graph of type affine
A

P_{1}
and

so that either they are dual to each other (rotation by

\pi
of

is
P_{1}
and of

is
Q_{1}
). We will call the former case

A consequence of Theorem
6.6
is that for the
\tilde{A}_{2n}
planar algebra
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
we cannot have the color case, whereas both cases will exist for the
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
planar algebra,
\mathcal{P}
. However, we will continue forward assuming the possibility for both cases for both
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
. Next we prove a collection of useful facts following from these decompositions of
X
.

Proof.

As
P_{1}
and
Q_{1}
are minimal projections,
P_{1}^{*}=P_{1}
and
Q_{1}^{*}=Q_{1}
, giving part (a) in both cases. For part (b), we can essentially follow the inner product computation done in Lemma
3.6
. For part (c) we follow a similar idea to Lemma
3.6
by defining
f
to be the upper strand of the leftmost diagram of the isomorphism. Finally, part (d) follows from taking the trace of
X=P_{1}+Q_{1}
and using that the trace of the minimal projections are 1.
∎

From the previous lemma we get that a for any diagram
T
, its adjoint,
T^{*}
, in the arrow case is vertically flip, reverse the arrows, and star the inside of any boxes, then extend this definition anti-linearly and on diagrams. For the color case,
T^{*}
is vertically flip and star the inside of any boxes.

The proof of the below lemma is nearly identical to the proofs of Lemma
3.8
and Lemma
3.9
and thus will be omitted.

Lemma 6.4
.

(i)

For
\mathcal{P}
with
n\geq 2
, using the labelling of the minimal projections in (
14
), we have that:

(a)

in the arrow case,
P_{k}\cong P_{1}^{\otimes k}
,
Q_{\ell}\cong Q_{1}^{\otimes\ell}
, and
P_{1}^{\otimes n}\cong Q_{1}^{\otimes n}
, and

(b)

in the color case,
P_{k}\cong P_{1}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes\overset{(k-1)}{...}\otimes R
,
Q_{\ell}\cong Q_{1}\otimes P_{1}\overset{(\ell-1)}{...}\otimes S
where
R,S
are
P_{1}
or
Q_{1}
depending on the parity of
k
and
\ell
. Further,
P_{1}\otimes Q_{1}\overset{(n-1)}{...}\otimes R\cong Q_{1}\otimes P_{1}\overset{(n-1)}{...}\otimes S
.

(ii)

For
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
, using the labelling of the minimal projections in (
16
), we have that in the arrow case,
P_{k}\cong P_{1}^{\otimes k}
,
Q_{\ell}\cong Q_{1}^{\otimes\ell}
,
P_{1}^{\otimes(n+1)}\cong Q_{1}^{\otimes n}
, and
P_{1}^{\otimes n}\cong Q_{1}^{\otimes(n+1)}
.

The above tells us the principal graphs for
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
and
\tilde{A}_{2n}
. For
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
in the arrow case we have principal graph

We are now ready to prove the necessary relations for any unshaded subfactor planar algebra with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
. Later in
7.12
we will prove that the elements listed in Definitions
6.1
and
6.3
are indeed generators of their respective planar algebra,
\mathcal{P}
. For now, we want to find elements and relations for the planar algebras.

Definition 6.1

(Elements in Affine
A
Unshaded Subfactor Planar Algebras: The Arrow Case)
.

We will show in the following that when
\text{ }\hbox to0.8pt{\vbox to20.72pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.4pt\lower-0.4pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.8pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 L 0 27.56}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

.

Theorem 6.5
.

(Necessary relations for
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
)

\mathcal{P}

1.

\mathcal{P}
has elements given in Definition
6.1
with relations given in Definition
6.2
. Further, we get the equivalence classes of minimal projections are for
n\geq 2
is (

n=1

6.3
with relations given in Definition
6.4
. Further, we get the equivalence classes of minimal projections are for
n\geq 2
, (
19
), and for

in
\mathcal{P}
where
UU^{*}=Q_{1}^{\otimes n}
and
U^{*}U=P_{1}^{\otimes n}
, which gives our U unitary relations.

For the final relation in the arrow case, notice that
\mathcal{F}(U)\in\text{Hom}\left(P_{1}^{\otimes n},Q_{1}^{\otimes n}\right)
. However, as
P_{1}^{\otimes n}\cong Q_{1}^{\otimes n}
and these elements are minimal projections, we get that
\text{dim}\left(\text{Hom}\left(P_{1}^{\otimes n},Q_{1}^{\otimes n}\right)\right)=1
. Thus,
\mathcal{F}(U)=\lambda U
for some
\lambda\in\mathbb{C}
. Applying
\mathcal{F}

2n
times we must circle back to
U
, so
\mathcal{F}^{2n}\left(U\right)=\lambda^{2n}U=U
. So
\lambda=\omega_{2n}
, some
2n
th root of unity. Noticing that
\mathcal{F}^{*}=\mathcal{F}^{-1}
gives that taking the star of
\mathcal{F}(U)=\lambda U
with
\lambda=\omega_{2n}
is
\mathcal{F}^{-1}(U^{*})=\omega_{2n}^{-1}U^{*}
. Applying
\mathcal{F}
to both sides gives
U^{*}=\omega_{2n}^{-1}\mathcal{F}(U^{*})
, which is the second click relation.

In the color case, there must exist morphisms, say
W\in\text{Hom}\left(\tilde{Q}_{1}\otimes\tilde{P}_{1}\overset{(n-1)}{...}\otimes S,\tilde{P}_{1}\otimes\tilde{Q}_{1}\overset{(n-1)}{...}\otimes R\right)
along with
W^{*}\in\text{Hom}\left(\tilde{P}_{1}\otimes\tilde{Q}_{1}\overset{(n-1)}{...}\otimes R,\tilde{Q}_{1}\otimes\tilde{P}_{1}\overset{(n-1)}{...}\otimes S\right)
, where
R,S\in\{\tilde{P}_{1},\tilde{Q}_{1}\}
,
R=P_{1}
only if
n
is odd, and
R\neq S
such that
W^{*}W=\tilde{Q}_{1}\otimes\tilde{P}_{1}\overset{(n-1)}{...}\otimes S
and
WW^{*}=\tilde{P}_{1}\otimes\tilde{Q}_{1}\overset{(n-1)}{...}\otimes R
. Since
\text{Hom}\left(\tilde{Q}_{1}\otimes\tilde{P}_{1}\overset{(n-1)}{...}\otimes S,\tilde{P}_{1}\otimes\tilde{Q}_{1}\overset{(n-1)}{...}\otimes R\right)
is one-dimensional, there exists
\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{C}
such that
\mathcal{F}(W)=\alpha W^{*}
and
\mathcal{F}(W^{*})=\beta W
. Taking
\mathcal{F}^{-1}
of both sides and moving the scalar over, we then get
\mathcal{F}^{-1}(W^{*})=\alpha^{-1}W
and
\mathcal{F}^{-1}(W)=\beta^{-1}W^{*}
. On the other hand, taking the adjoint of both sides of the equalities:
\mathcal{F}(W)=\alpha W^{*}
and
\mathcal{F}(W^{*})=\beta W
and noticing
\mathcal{F}(W)^{*}=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(W^{*})
and
\mathcal{F}(W^{*})^{*}=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(W)
gives that
\mathcal{F}^{-1}(W^{*})=\overline{\alpha}W
and
\mathcal{F}^{-1}(W)=\overline{\beta}W^{*}
. Therefore,
\alpha^{-1}=\overline{\alpha}
and
\beta^{-1}=\overline{\beta}
.

We can further show that
\alpha\beta=\tau_{n}
, some
n
th root of unity. Notice that
\mathcal{F}^{2}(W)=(\alpha\beta)W
and applying
\mathcal{F}^{2}

n
times we must circle back to
W
, so
\mathcal{F}^{2n}(W)=(\alpha\beta)^{n}W=W
and
\alpha\beta
must be an
n
th root of unity.

Define the morphism
V
, shown below, by
V=\sqrt{\alpha}W^{*}
, making
V^{*}=\overline{\sqrt{\alpha}}W=\sqrt{\alpha^{-1}}W
, which is also shown below

Thus
VV^{*}=\tilde{Q}_{1}\otimes\tilde{P}_{1}\overset{(n-1)}{...}\otimes S
and
V^{*}V=\tilde{P}_{1}\otimes\tilde{Q}_{1}\overset{(n-1)}{...}\otimes R
, giving relation (v). Further, for the
n
th root of unity
\tau_{n}=\alpha\beta
,

\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(V)=\sqrt{\alpha}\beta W=\alpha\beta\sqrt{\alpha^{-1}}W=\alpha\beta V^{*}=\tau_{n}V^{*},\text{ and }\tau_{n}\mathcal{F}^{-1}(V)=\beta\sqrt{\alpha}W=\beta\alpha\sqrt{\alpha^{-1}}W=\alpha\beta V^{*}

proving relation (vi). Thus we have shown that
\mathcal{P}
must have all of the given elements and relations. ∎

We will show in
7.12
that the elements
P_{1}
,
U
, and
U^{*}
from the preceding are indeed generators of
\mathcal{P}
. Next we tackle the
\tilde{A}_{2n}
. The following is nearly identical to the arrow case of
6.5
so will be omitted.

Theorem 6.6
.

(Necessary relations for
\tilde{A}_{2n}
). Fix
n\in\mathbb{N}
. If
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
is an unshaded subfactor planar algebra with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n}
, then
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
has elements given in Definition
6.1
and relations given in Definition
6.2
except with
U
having
n+1
strands on the bottom and
U^{*}
having
n+1
strands on top. Further we get the equivalence classes of minimal projections are given in (
21
).

From this, the following remark is immediate.

Remark 6.1
.

In
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
, we cannot have that
P_{1}
and
Q_{1}
are self-dual.

Remark 6.2
.

Just as in the shaded case, we can always oriented a strand in its entirety using strand decomposition and orientation disagreement.

We will show in
7.12
that elements
P_{1}
,
U
, and
U^{*}
in the previous generate
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
.

7
Sufficient Relations for Affine
A
Finite Unshaded Planar Algebras: The Arrow Case

In this section we start with generators and relations for a planar algebra and prove that it generates an unshaded subfactor planar algebra and further this planar algebra has an affine
A
principal graph. Depending on the choice of root of unity and the number of strands around the generator boxes, these planar algebras could either have
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
or
\tilde{A}_{2n}
Dynkin diagram as its principal graph.

Theorem 7.1
.

(Sufficient relations for
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
and
\tilde{A}_{2n}
: Arrow case) Fix
n\in\mathbb{N}
and a
2n
th root of unity
\omega_{2n}
(respectively, a
2n+1
root of unity
\omega_{2n+1}
for
\tilde{A}_{2n}
). Let
\mathcal{P}
be the planar algebra generated by
P_{1}
,
U
,
U^{*}
from Definition
6.1
with relations from Definition
6.2
. Let
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
be defined the same as
\mathcal{P}
except with
U
having
n+1
strands on the bottom and
U^{*}
having
n+1
strands on top. Define
P_{1}
to be self-adjoint,
U^{*}
to be the adjoint of
U
, and extend * anti-linearly and on diagrams. Then
\mathcal{P}
(respectively,
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
) is an unshaded subfactor planar algebra whose principal graph is the
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
(respectively,
\tilde{A}_{2n}
) Dynkin diagram, given by, for
n\geq 2
by (
17
) and when
n=1
by (
18
) (respectively, (
21
) for
\tilde{A}_{2n}
.)

Fix
n\in\mathbb{N}
, a
2n
th root of unity
\omega_{2n}
, and a
2n+1
th root of unity
\omega_{2n+1}
. Sometimes we will use
\omega
to mean either
\omega_{2n}
or
\omega_{2n+1}
when the context is clear. Throughout the rest of this section,
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
will refer to the planar algebra defined through generators and relations given in the previous theorem . We will denote the
k

\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
as
\mathcal{P}_{k}
and
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{k}
respectively. While dealing with the arrow case, define

}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{{{}{}{{}}
}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{{{}{}{{}}

\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {{

Before proving Theorem
7.1
, we will prove some claims about
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
. Most of the proofs we will just prove for
\mathcal{P}
. Adapting the proofs for
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
mostly involves adjusting some
n
to be
n+1
but are otherwise identical. If there is more work than that to adjust, we will include it.

As
*
is defined to be extended anti-linearly and on diagrams, it is clear that for any diagram
T
in the planar algebra,
T^{*}
is vertically flipping, reversing the arrows, and switching
U
and
U^{*}
. It is left to check that the * is well-defined by checking it respects the defining relations of the planar algebra.

Lemma 7.2
.

The adjoint is well-defined.

Proof.

From the preceding paragraph,
*
respects the bubble relations, strand decomposition, orientation disagreement, saddle relations, and the
U
unitary relation clearly. For the click relations, notice that taking the adjoint of the first relation gives
\mathcal{F}(U)^{*}=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(U^{*})=\omega^{-1}U^{*}
. Then taking
\mathcal{F}
of second equality gives
U^{*}=\omega^{-1}\mathcal{F}(U)
, which gives the second click relation. Similarly, taking the adjoint of the second click relation will give the first click relation. ∎

As done for shaded planar algebras, we start by showing that the 0-box spaces are one-dimensional. Again, we use a standard fact from the theory of van Kampen diagrams which we state in the following remark.

Remark 7.1
.

For any diagram in
\mathcal{P}
(respectively
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
) there exists a unique function from the regions of the diagram to the cyclic group
\mathbb{Z}_{2n}=\langle u|u^{2n}=1\rangle
(respectively
\mathbb{Z}_{2n+1}
) such that the region on the left-most boundary next to the star is assigned 1 and neighboring regions are assigened elements from the group in the following way. If on the left-side from the point of view of the arrow the region is labelled
x
, then the region on the right is labelled
xu
.

We first show
\mathcal{P}_{0}
is at least one-dimensional by defining a surjection from
\mathcal{P}_{0}
to
\mathbb{C}
.

Define a function
f_{U}:\mathcal{P}_{0}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}
by the following algorithm. By strand decomposition and orientation disagreement it suffices to define
f_{U}
on diagrams where every strand is oriented in on direction in its entirety and then extend
f_{U}
linearly. Let
D\in\mathcal{P}_{0}
be such a diagram.

1.

If there are no
U
and
U^{*}
s in
D
, define
f_{U}(D)=1
.

2.

If there are
U
or
U^{*}
s in
D
, enumerate all of the
U
and
U^{*}
, say
U_{1},...,U_{r}
, and
U^{*}_{1},...,U^{*}_{s}
. (Note that
r=s
but we do not need this fact.)

3.

Define a number
\ell_{j}^{J}
based on the following table where
w_{j}^{J}
is the element of
\mathbb{Z}_{2n}
that corresponds to the region where
J_{j}
’s star lies.

When
J=U

When
J=U^{*}
,

\bullet
if
w_{j}^{J}=u^{m}
, then
\ell_{j}^{J}=-m
,

\bullet
if
w_{j}^{J}=u^{m}
, then
\ell_{j}^{J}=m

4.

Define
\ell^{D}=\left(\sum_{j=1}^{s}\ell_{j}^{U^{*}}-\sum_{i=1}^{r}\ell_{i}^{U}\right)(\text{mod }2n)
.

5.

Then define
f_{U}(D)=\omega_{2n}^{\ell^{D}}
and extend
f_{U}
linearly to define all of
f_{U}
.

For
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
use
\omega_{2n+1}
and take the length mod
2n+1
instead. To show
f_{U}
is well-defined we need to show that
f_{U}
does not depend on the path chosen and is invariant under the defining relations of the planar algebra.

Lemma 7.3
.

f_{U}
is well defined.

Proof.

To show the lemma, we must prove
f_{U}
respects the defining relations of
\mathcal{P}
(or
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
). Without loss of generality, consider
\mathcal{P}
. Let
D
and
D^{\prime}
be two diagrams in
\mathcal{P}_{0}
that are identical except in a local region.

Most of this proof is identical to the proof of Lemma
4.3
. What’s left to check is the unitary relations and the click relations.

Let
D
and
D^{\prime}
be identical except in a local region
D
is the middle equality of the
UU^{*}
relation (i.e., written with two boxes) and
D^{\prime}
is the right-hand side (written with no boxes). The top and bottom boundary data is the same, so any region above or below the the local regions are labelled the same. Therefore the entire diagrams are labelled identically. Further, in the local region of
D
,
U
and
U^{*}
’s
\ell
-values cancel, giving that
f_{U}
is invariant under this unitary relation. The same argument works for
U^{*}U
.

Lastly, we check that
f_{U}
is invariant under the click relations. We just check the first click relation. The other is the same process. Let
D
have a local region that looks like the first diagram of the first click relation and
D^{\prime}
have a region that looks like
U
. It is clear that outside this region both
D
and
D^{\prime}
are labelled identically.

Suppose the word at the left-side of the local region is
x
. The word associated to the
U
box in the local region of
D
is
xu^{-1}
. In
D^{\prime}
the word associated to the region is
x
. Thus the
\ell
-value associated to the box of
D
is one more than of
D^{\prime}
. Thus, when multiplying
D^{\prime}
by
\omega
, we get the same value of
f
as
D
.

Hence we have shown that
f_{U}
is invariant under the relations of
\mathcal{P}
. This concludes showing that
f_{U}
is well-defined. ∎

Corollary 7.4
.

\mathcal{P}_{0}
and
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{0}
are at least 1-dimensional.

Proof.

We have well-defined functions from
\mathcal{P}_{0}
to
\mathbb{C}
and
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{0}
to
\mathbb{C}
. These functions send
\emptyset
to 1 and are linear. Therefore, the maps are surjections, which implies that the 0-box spaces are at least one-dimensional. ∎

Now I will show that
\mathcal{P}_{0}
and
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{0}
are at most 1-dimensional, by defining an evaluation algorithm.

Evaluation Algorithm for
\mathcal{P}_{0}
:

By strand decomposition and orientation disagreement it suffices to define the algorithm on diagrams where every strand is oriented in one direction in its entirety then extend linearly. Let
D\in\mathcal{P}_{0}
be such a diagram.

1.

If
D
has no
U
or
U^{*}
, skip to step 6. Now assume
D
has some
U
or
U^{*}
. Since
D
is nontrivial, this
U
or
U^{*}
cannot have a cap or cup. The diagram is closed, so the strands of
U
or
U^{*}
cannot go to the boundary of
D
. Due to orientation, the strands of
U
cannot connect to another
U
and similarly, the strands of
U^{*}
cannot connect to another
U^{*}
. Thus, if
D
has a
U
, the strands of
U
must connect to a
U^{*}
and if
D
has a
U^{*}
, the strands of
U^{*}
must connect to a
U
. Thus we can assume
D
has both a
U
and
U^{*}
and all the strands of
U
connect to
U^{*}
s and the strands of
U^{*}
all connect to
U
s.

2.

Pick any
U
and
U^{*}
connected by at least one strand. We will inductively increase the number of strands connecting
U
and
U^{*}
. If
U
and
U^{*}
are connected by only 1 strand, then use the click relation to have
U
and
U^{*}
connected by the top left strand of the left box is connected by the top right strand of the right box. So your diagram is multiplied by some factor of
\omega_{2n}
.

3.

For the strand of
U
adjacent to the connected strand, isotope the strand so that it lies next to the strand of
U^{*}
adjacent to the connected strand. Then use the saddle relation to make
U
and
U^{*}
connected by at least 2 adjacent strands.

4.

Inductively repeat the process until
U
and
U^{*}
are connected by
s<n
adjacent strands. It is clear that we can then repeat the process of step 4 and get
U
and
U^{*}
connected by
n
adjacent strands.

5.

Use the
U
and
U^{*}
relation to reduce
D
to have one less
U
and
U^{*}
. Repeat steps 2-6 until no more
U
and
U^{*}
remain.

6.

Now
D
is a closed diagram consisting of only oriented loops multiplied by some scalars. Starting with an innermost loop, repeatedly pop the loops for a factor of 1 using that an oriented loop evaluates to 1.
D
will then evaluate to a multiple of
\emptyset
and thus we can evaluate on all of
\mathcal{P}_{0}
.

The evaluation algorithm of
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{0}
is nearly identical, just exchanging
\omega_{2n}
with
\omega_{2n+1}
and change appropriate
n
s with
n+1
. With the evaluation algorithm the following lemma is immediate.

Lemma 7.5
.

\mathcal{P}_{0}
and
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{0}
are at most one-dimensional.

With the well-defined surjection,
f_{U}
, the following corollary is immediate.

Corollary 7.6
.

\mathcal{P}_{0}
and
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{0}
are one-dimensional.

Lemma 7.7
.

In both
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
,
P_{1}\otimes Q_{1}\cong\emptyset
and
Q_{1}\otimes P_{1}\cong\emptyset
.

Proof.

We prove the first isomorphism. The other can be found similarly. Define

by the bubble relations. ∎

Lemma 7.8
.

For all
0\leq k\leq n
,

(i)

in
\mathcal{P}
,
P_{1}^{\otimes(2n-k)}\cong Q_{1}^{\otimes k}
, and

(ii)

in
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
,
P_{1}^{\otimes(2n+1-k)}\cong Q_{1}^{\otimes k}
.

Proof.

Both planar algebras will follow the same proof, so we just prove the lemma for
\mathcal{P}
. Notice that
P_{1}^{\otimes n}\cong Q_{1}^{\otimes n}
, as we can let
f=U
and
f^{*}=U^{*}
, and by the defining relations
ff^{*}\cong Q_{1}^{\otimes n}
and
f^{*}f\cong P_{1}^{\otimes n}
. Let
k\geq 0
. Tensor
n-k
copies of
P_{1}
on the right of both sides of the isomorphism
P_{1}^{\otimes n}\cong Q_{1}^{\otimes n}
. The left-hand side is
P_{1}^{\otimes(2n-k)}
and the right-hand side, using Lemma
7.7
, is
Q_{1}^{\otimes k}
, which gives the desired isomorphism. ∎

Lemma 7.9
.

The principal graph of
\mathcal{P}
is (
17
) when
n\geq 2
and (
18
) when
n=1
. The principal graph of
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
is (
21
).

Proof.

Without loss of generality, we prove the result for
\mathcal{P}
. Define
P_{k}=P_{1}^{\otimes k}
for
1\leq k\leq n
and
Q_{\ell}=Q_{1}^{\otimes\ell}
for
1\leq\ell\leq n-1
. First I show that for all
1\leq k\leq n
,
\text{dim}(\text{Hom}\left(P_{k},P_{k}\right))=1
and for all
1\leq\ell\leq n-1
,
\text{dim}\left(\text{Hom}\left(Q_{\ell},Q_{\ell}\right)\right)=1
. For any
P_{k}
, pick
f\in\text{Hom}(P_{k},P_{k})
. Diagrammatically we have:

f
…
(
k
)
…
(
k
)
.

Then isotope a string to be adjacent to an oppositely-oriented one and use the saddle relation in the following manner:

f
…
(
k-1
)
…
(
k
)

\mapsto

f
…
(
k-1
)
…
(
k-1
)

.

Continuing in this fashion we get
\text{tr}(f)\otimes P_{k}
.

As we can evaluate any closed diagram by Lemma
7.6
, we get that there exists some scalar
\lambda\in\mathbb{C}
, such that this diagram is equivalent to
\lambda P_{k}
. Thus
\text{dim}(\text{Hom}(P_{k},P_{k})\leq 1
for all
1\leq k\leq n
. Since tr
(P_{k})=1
this gives that
\text{dim}(\text{Hom}(P_{k},P_{k}))=1
for all
1\leq k\leq n
. A similar argument can be done to show
\text{dim}(\text{Hom}(Q_{\ell},Q_{\ell}))=1
for all
1\leq\ell\leq n-1
.

Next we want to show that
P_{k}
and
Q_{\ell}
are projections for all
1\leq k\leq n
,
1\leq\ell\leq n-1
. Indeed, multiplication is vertical stacking, so
P_{k}^{2}=P_{k}
for all
1\leq k\leq n
and
Q_{\ell}^{2}=Q_{\ell}
for all
1\leq\ell\leq n-1
is clear. Recall that we define
P_{1}^{*}=P_{1}
which gives that
Q_{1}^{*}=Q_{1}
. We then obtain that
P_{k}^{*}=P_{k}
and
Q_{\ell}^{*}=Q_{\ell}
for all
1\leq k\leq n
and
1\leq\ell\leq n-1
and these elements are all projections. Using the previous paragraph, these projections will all be minimal.

Now we show that these projections are nonisomorphic by showing there are no nontrivial morphism between any of two distinct minimal projections we have defined. We break this into cases dependent on the orientations of the distinct projections.

Case 1:
Suppose
P_{k}
and
Q_{\ell}
(
1\leq k\leq n
,
1\leq\ell\leq n-1
) are two projections for distinct vertices and let
X\in\text{Hom}(Q_{\ell},P_{k})
. Use the strand decomposition and orientation disagreement to rewrite
X
as a summand of morphisms from
P_{k}
to
Q_{\ell}
with all oriented strands and without loss of generality, no closed components. Let
X^{\prime}
be some such summand. Diagrammatrically we have:

(22)

For
X^{\prime}
suppose there are
k_{1}

U
s and
k_{2}

U^{*}
s. On the boundary of a
U
-box there are
2n
sinks and on the boundary of a
U^{*}
-box there are
2n
sources. Let
m
be the number of strands in
X^{\prime}
, which means there are
m
total sinks either on the boundary of
X^{\prime}
or inside
X^{\prime}
(and thus on a
U
-box) and
m
total sources (which must happen on a
U^{*}
-box). As
P_{k}
has
k
sinks on the boundary of
X^{\prime}
and
Q_{\ell}
has
\ell
sinks on the boundary of
X^{\prime}
,
m=k+\ell+2k_{1}n=2k_{2}n
. Therefore,
(k+\ell)\equiv 0(\text{mod }2n)
. However,
1\leq k\leq n
and
1\leq\ell\leq n-1
, which gives there is no solution and thus no nonzero
X^{\prime}
. So
\text{dim}(\text{Hom}(Q_{\ell},P_{k}))=\text{dim}(\text{Hom}(P_{k},Q_{\ell}))=0
for all
1\leq k\leq n
and
1\leq\ell\leq n-1
.

Case 2:
Suppose
P_{k}
and
P_{\ell}
are two projections for distinct vertices and let
1\leq\ell<k\leq n
. Let
X\in\text{Hom}(P_{\ell},P_{k})
. Again, use the strand decomposition and that the 0-box space is 1-dimensional to rewrite
X
as a summand of morphisms from
P_{k}
to
P_{\ell}
with all oriented strands and no closed components. Let
X^{\prime}
be some such summand. Diagrammatically we have the same as (
22
) except the orientation of the arrows at the top are reversed.

From
P_{k}
there are
k
sinks on the boundary of
X^{\prime}
and from
P_{\ell}
there are
\ell
sources on the boundary of
X^{\prime}
. Let
m
be the number of strands in
X^{\prime}
, which is also the number of sources and sinks. Let
X^{\prime}
have
k_{1}

U
-boxes and
k_{2}

U^{*}
-boxes. Then
m=k+2k_{1}n=\ell+2k_{2}n
, so
k-\ell\equiv 0(\text{ mod}2n)
. As
1\leq\ell<k\leq n
, we again get that there is no solution and no nonzero
X^{\prime}
. Therefore,
\text{dim}(\text{Hom}(P_{k},P_{\ell}))=0
for distinct
k
and
\ell
from 1 to
n
.

The next case is to show
\text{dim}(\text{Hom}(Q_{k},Q_{\ell}))=0
for distinct
k
and
\ell
from 1 to
n-1
. However, this argument is nearly identical to Case 2, and thus is omitted.

The final case is to show
\text{dim}(\text{Hom}(P,\emptyset))=0
for all
P\in\{P_{k},Q_{\ell}:1\leq k\leq n,1\leq\ell\leq n-1\}
. Without loss of generality suppose
P=P_{k}
for some fixed
k\in\{1,...,n\}
and let
f\in\text{Hom}(\emptyset,P_{k})
. Suppose there are
m
strands in
f
,
k_{1}

U
-boxes, and
k_{2}

U^{*}
-boxes. Then
m
is the number of sinks in
f
which is
2nk_{1}
and it also equals the number of sources in
f
which is
2nk_{2}+k
. Therefore
k\equiv 0(\text{ mod}2n)
. There is no such
k
such that this is true, and so
\text{dim}(\text{Hom}(P_{k},\emptyset))=0
as desired.

Therefore,
\text{dim}(\text{Hom}(P,Q))=0
for all distinct minimal projections
P,Q\in\{P_{k},Q_{\ell}:1\leq k\leq n,1\leq\ell\leq n-1\}
. Thus all our minimal projections defined are nonisomorphic.

Finally, what’s left to show the tensor decomposition. The first relation
X\cong\emptyset\otimes X\cong P_{1}\oplus Q_{1}
is given by the strand decomposition. Fix
k\in\mathbb{N}
where
0<k<n-1
. Then using Lemma
7.7
,

\displaystyle P_{k}\otimes X=P_{1}^{\otimes k}\otimes X\cong P_{1}^{\otimes k}\otimes\left(P_{1}\oplus Q_{1}\right)\cong\left(P_{1}^{\otimes(k+1)}\right)\oplus\left(P_{1}^{\otimes k}\otimes Q_{1}\right)\cong\left(P_{1}^{\otimes(k+1)}\right)\oplus\left(P_{1}^{\otimes(k-1)}\right)=P_{k+1}\oplus P_{k-1}

Similarly,
Q_{\ell}\otimes X\cong Q_{\ell+1}\oplus Q_{\ell-1}
.

For the last vertex, using Lemma
7.8
,

\displaystyle P_{n}\otimes X=P_{1}^{\otimes n}\otimes X

\displaystyle\cong P_{1}^{\otimes n}\otimes\left(P_{1}\oplus Q_{1}\right)\cong\left(P_{1}^{\otimes(n+1)}\right)\oplus\left(P_{1}^{\otimes n}\otimes Q_{1}\right)\cong\left(Q_{1}^{\otimes n}\otimes P_{1}\right)\oplus\left(P_{1}^{\otimes(n-1)}\right)\cong\left(Q_{1}^{\otimes(n-1)}\right)\oplus\left(P_{1}^{\otimes(n-1)}\right)

which equals
P_{n-1}\oplus Q_{n-1}
. So
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
indeed is the principal graph representing the tensor decomposition. ∎

Next, we need to show that our generators and relations are sufficient to ensure sphericality. However this proof is essentially done in Lemma
4.9
so will be omitted.

Lemma 7.10
.

\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
are spherical.

To conclude showing that
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
are
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
unshaded subfactor planar algebra we have one final requirement; we need to show they are positive definite.

Lemma 7.11
.

\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
are positive definite.

Proof.

As done in Lemma
3.4
we use the explicit positive definite basis given in
[
MPS10
]
. The only thing left to verify is that he minimal projections have positive trace. It is easy to see that all minimal projections have trace 1, so both planar algebras are positive definite. ∎

Proof of Theorem
7.1
.

All of the work has already been done. Fix an
n\in\mathbb{N}
. From Lemma
7.6
, we get that the space of closed diagrams is 1-dimensional. Lemma
7.10
gives that
\mathcal{P}
is spherical and Lemma
7.9
gives that the principal graph of
\mathcal{P}
is the
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
Dynkin diagram. Finally, we get that
\mathcal{P}
is positive definite from Lemma
7.11
, which completes the proof. ∎

Theorem 7.12
.

The elements
P_{1}
,
U
, and
U^{*}
from Definition
6.1
generate
\mathcal{P}
in the arrow case of Theorem
6.5
. The elements
P_{1}
,
U
, and
U^{*}
from Definition
6.1
except with
U
having
n+1
strands on the bottom and
U^{*}
have
n+1
strands on top generate
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
from Theorem
6.6
.

Proof.

Nearly identical to the proof of Theorem
4.11
. ∎

8
Sufficient Relations for Affine
A
Finite Unshaded Planar Algebras: The Color Case

As done with the arrow case, we can find that the color relations given in Theorem
6.5
also are sufficient for defining the
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
unshaded subfactor planar algebra. Recall that there is no
\tilde{A}_{2n}
unshaded subfactor planar algebra.

Theorem 8.1
.

(Sufficient relations for
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
: Color case) Fix
n\in\mathbb{N}
and an
n
th root of unity
\tau_{n}
. Let
\mathcal{P}
be the planar algebra generated by
P_{1},Q_{1},V,
and
V^{*}
from Definition
6.3
with relations from Definition
6.4
. Define
P_{1}
and
Q_{1}
to be self-adjoint,
V^{*}
to the be adjoint of
V
and extend * anti-linearly and on diagrams. Then
\mathcal{P}
is an unshaded subfactor planar algebra whose principal graph is given by (
19
) when
n\geq 2
and (
20
) when
n=1
.

Fix
n\in\mathbb{N}
and an
n
th root of unity,
\tau_{n}
. Throughout the rest of this section,
\mathcal{P}
will denote the planar algebra defined by generators and relations in the above theorem. Denote the
k
-th box space as
\mathcal{P}_{k}
. Our strategy is similar as in the arrow case. Before proving Theorem
8.1
, we will prove some claims about
\mathcal{P}
.

As the adjoint is defined to be extended anti-linearly and on diagrams, it is clear that for any diagram
T\in\mathcal{P}
that for any diagram
T
,
T^{*}
is obtained by vertically flipping and switching
V
and
V^{*}
.

Lemma 8.2
.

The adjoint is well-defined.

Proof.

From the preceding paragraph, * clearly respects the bubble relations, strand decomposition, color disagreement, saddle relations, and the
V
unitary relations.

Before proving that the adjoint respect the click relation we show other equalities that must hold from the click relation. For the click relation:
\mathcal{F}(V)=\tau_{n}V^{*}=\tau_{n}\mathcal{F}^{-1}(V)
, taking
\mathcal{F}^{-1}
of the first equality gives
V=\tau_{n}\mathcal{F}^{-1}(V^{*})
and taking
\mathcal{F}
of the second equality gives
\tau_{n}\mathcal{F}(V^{*})=\tau_{n}V
. Then we can see that taking the adjoint of the click relation gives
\mathcal{F}^{-1}(V^{*})=\tau_{n}^{-1}V=\tau_{n}^{-1}\mathcal{F}(V^{*})

which is indeed true in the planar algebra. Thus the adjoint is well-defined. ∎

To tackle showing that
\text{dim}(\mathcal{P}_{0})=1
, we first show
\mathcal{P}_{0}
is at least one-dimensional by defining a surjection from
\mathcal{P}_{0}
into
\mathbb{C}
then show it is at most one-dimensional by giving an evaluation algorithm. Fortunately, our map is nearly identical to the function
f:\mathcal{P}_{0}\to\mathbb{C}
given in section

4
. Recall that
f
never took into consideration the shading of the diagrams. With this in mind, we define
f_{V}
.

Define
f_{V}:\mathcal{P}_{0}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}
by plugging
D\in\mathcal{P}_{0}
into
f
but recording red strands as
b
and blue strands as
r
.

Lemma 8.3
.

f_{V}
is a well-defined function.

Proof.

We need to verify that
f_{V}
is invariant under the relations of
\mathcal{P}
. The bubble relations, color disagreement, saddle relations, and unitary relations follow the same reasoning as Lemma
4.3
.

Finally, we check that
f_{V}
respects the click relation. Let
D
,
D^{\prime}
, and
D^{\prime\prime}
be identical closed diagrams except locally
D
has a
V^{*}
where
D^{\prime}
has a
\mathcal{F}^{-1}(V)
and
D^{\prime\prime}
has a
\mathcal{F}(V)
. It is clear that the regions outside of this local neighborhood will all have the same labellings.

Suppose the group element on the left-hand side of the neighborhood is
x
. We break this up into cases.

Case 1
: Suppose
x=(rb)^{m}
for
m\in\mathbb{Z}
. Then the corresponding
\ell
-value for the
V^{*}
in
D
will be
-m
. For
D^{\prime}
, the region of
V
’s star will be the group element
xr=r(br)^{m}
, giving an
\ell
-value of
-m
. In
D^{\prime\prime}
, the region will associated to
V
will be labelled
r(br)^{m-1}
and thus the
\ell
-value of
V
will be of
-(m-1)
.

Case 2
: Suppose
x=(br)^{m}
. Then the corresponding
\ell
-value for the
V^{*}
in
D
will be
m
. In
D^{\prime}
the
V
-box’s star’s region will now be labelled
b(rb)^{m-1}
. So the
V
-box will have
\ell
-value of
m
. Now consider the
V
-box in
D^{\prime\prime}
. The region associated to the
V
’s star will be labelled
b(rb)^{m}
, so the corresponding
\ell
-value will be
m+1
.

Case 3
: Suppose
x=r(br)^{m}
. Then the corresponding
\ell
-value for
D
will be
m
. In
D^{\prime}
the
V
-box’s star’s region will be labelled
(rb)^{m}
, giving an
\ell
-value of
m
. For
D^{\prime\prime}
, the
V
-box’s star will be labelled
(rb)^{m+1}
, giving an
\ell
-value of
m+1
.

Case 4
: Suppose
x=b(rb)^{m}
. For
D
the corresponding
\ell
-value for
V^{*}
will be
-(m+1)
. In
D^{\prime}
the region is now labelled
(br)^{m+1}
, giving an
\ell
-value of
-(m+1)
. Now for
D^{\prime\prime}
the region for
V
’s star will be labelled
(br)^{m}
, which will give that
V
-box an
\ell
-value of
-m
.

This concludes showing that
f_{V}
is well-defined. ∎

Lemma 8.4
.

\mathcal{P}_{0}
is at least one-dimensional.

Proof.

By the preceding lemma,
f_{V}
is well-defined. Further,
f_{V}(\emptyset)=1
and is a linear map,
f_{V}
is surjective. So
\mathcal{P}_{0}
is at least 1-dimensional. ∎

To show that
\mathcal{P}_{0}
is at most one-dimensional, we can define an evaluation algorithm. Again, noticing that the evaluation algorithm in the shaded planar algebra case did not depend on shading, we can just follow the steps of the evaluation algorithm in section
4
. That is:

The Evaluation Algorithm for
\mathcal{P}_{0}
:

Follow the steps of the evaluation algorithm of the shaded planar algebra in section
4
, ignoring any reference to
U
or
U^{*}
-boxes and shading.

Lemma 8.5
.

\mathcal{P}_{0}
is one-dimensional.

Proof.

From Lemma
8.4
, we know
\text{dim}(\mathcal{P}_{0})
is at least one-dimensional. As we have an evaluation algorithm, we get that every element
D\in\mathcal{P}_{0}
can be rewritten as a scalar multiple of
\emptyset
, therefore,
\mathcal{P}_{0}
is at most one-dimensional, giving the result. ∎

We want to then show that the
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
Dynkin diagram is the correct principal graph for this planar algebra. However this result follows from a similar process to Lemmas
3.6
and
4.8
which gives:

Lemma 8.6
.

The principal graph of
\mathcal{P}
is given by the Dynkin diagrams in the right-hand column of Theorem
6.5
.

Following the proof of Lemma
4.9
, we get

Lemma 8.7
.

\mathcal{P}
is spherical.

Lemma 8.8
.

\mathcal{P}
is positive definite.

Proof.

This is nearly the same as the proof as Lemma
8.8
. The only thing left to check is that the minimal projections have positive trace. However, we know every minimal projection has trace equal to 1, so
\mathcal{P}
is indeed positive definite. ∎

Proof of Theorem
8.1
.

All of the work has already been done. Fix
n\in\mathbb{N}
. From Lemma
8.5
we get that the space of closed diagrams is 1-dimensional. Lemma
8.7
gives that
\mathcal{P}
is spherical and Lemma
8.6
gives that the principal graph of
\mathcal{P}
is the
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
Dynkin diagram. Finally, we get that
\mathcal{P}
is positive definite from Lemma
8.8
, which completes the proof. ∎

Theorem 8.9
.

The elements
P_{1},Q_{1},V,
and
V^{*}
from Definition
6.3
generate
\mathcal{P}
in the color case of Theorem
6.5
.

Proof.

Follow Theorem
4.11
. ∎

Theorem 9.1
.

There are exactly
3n
nonisomorphic unshaded subfactor planar algebras with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
.

First, we will prove that none of the arrow case presentations are isomorphic to the color case presentations. Then we will prove that the
2n
and
n
presentations in the respective presentations are distinct.

Lemma 9.2
.

Fix
n\in\mathbb{N}
. All of the
2n
planar algebras given by presentations in the arrow case for
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
are nonisomorphic to each of the
n
planar algebras given by presentations in the color case for
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
.

Proof.

Let
\mathcal{P}
be a presentation of an arrow case with chosen
2n
th root of unity
\omega_{2n}
for
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
and
\mathcal{Q}
be a presentation of the color case with chosen
n
th root of unity
\tau_{n}
. Suppose for contradiction that there exists an isomorphism
\theta:\mathcal{P}\rightarrow\mathcal{Q}
. Recalling the definition of planar algebra isomorphism, there exists a bijective map
\theta_{1}:\mathcal{P}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{Q}_{1}
. A planar algebra isomorphism preserves minimal projections so either
\theta_{1}(P^{\prime}_{1})=P_{1}
and
\theta_{1}(Q_{1})=Q^{\prime}_{1}
or
\theta_{1}(P_{1})=Q^{\prime}_{1}
and
\theta(Q_{1})=P^{\prime}_{1}
.

Let
T
be the click tangle in the 1-box space. Then
Z_{T}\left(\theta_{1}\left(P_{1}\right)\right)=\theta_{1}(P_{1})
since in
\mathcal{Q}
both
P^{\prime}_{1}
and
Q^{\prime}_{1}
are self-dual. As
\theta_{1}
is an isomorphism this is equal to
\theta_{1}\left(Z_{T}\left(P_{1}\right)\right)=\theta_{1}\left(Q_{1}\right)
. Therefore
\theta_{1}\left(P_{1}\right)=\theta_{1}\left(Q_{1}\right)
, which is a contradiction. Hence there is no isomorphism between
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{Q}
. ∎

Lemma 9.3
.

Fix
n\in\mathbb{N}
.

(i)

Let
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{Q}
be planar algebras given by generators from Definition
6.1
and relations from Definition
6.2
using
2n
th roots of unity
\omega_{1}
and
\omega_{2}
respectively. If
\omega_{1}\neq\omega_{2}
then
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{Q}
are nonisomorphic.

(ii)

Let
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{Q}
be planar algebras given by generators from Definition
6.3
with relations from Definition
6.2
using
n
th roots of unity
\tau_{1}
and
\tau_{2}
respectively. If
\tau_{1}\neq\tau_{2}
then
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{Q}
are nonisomorphic.

Proof.

For sake of contradiction let
\theta:\mathcal{P}\rightarrow\mathcal{Q}
be an isomorphism where
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{Q}
are planar algebra with presentations given in the arrow case with chosen distinct
2n
th roots of unity
\omega_{1}
and
\omega_{2}
respectively. Call the
U
-box of
\mathcal{P}

U
and the
U
-box of
\mathcal{Q}

U^{\prime}
. Call the distinct minimal projections in the 1-box space of
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathcal{Q}
both
P_{1}
and
Q_{1}
. However, it should be clear from context which planar algebra these projections lie in. By definition of planar algebra isomorphism,
\theta_{1}:\mathcal{P}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{Q}_{1}
is a bijective map between the 1-box spaces. As planar algebra isomorphisms preserve minimal projections, either
\theta_{1}(P_{1})=P_{1}
and
\theta_{1}(Q_{1})=Q_{1}
or
\theta_{1}(P_{1})=Q_{1}
and
\theta_{1}(Q_{1})=P_{1}
.

A planar algebra isomorphism also preserves the tensor product. So when
\theta_{1}(P_{1})=P_{1}
,
\theta(U)\in\text{Hom}\left(P_{1}^{\otimes n},Q_{1}^{\otimes n}\right)
. Therefore
\theta(U)
is a multiple of
U^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{Q}
. When
\theta_{1}(P_{1})=Q_{1}
, we get that
\theta(U)
is a multiple of
U^{\prime*}
.

We then conclude that
\omega_{1}=\omega_{2}
. In the case where
\theta_{1}(P_{1})=P_{1}
we get that there exists a
\lambda\in\mathbb{C}
such that
\theta(U)=\lambda U^{\prime}
. Let
T=\mathcal{F}
be the click tangle in the
n
-box space. Then
Z_{T}(\theta(U))=Z_{T}(\lambda U^{\prime})=\lambda Z_{T}(U^{\prime})=\lambda\omega_{2}U^{\prime}
which is the same as
\theta(Z_{T}(U))=\theta(\omega_{1}U)=\omega_{1}\theta(U)=\omega_{1}\lambda U^{\prime}
. This gives that
\omega_{1}=\omega_{2}
, contradicting that
\omega_{1}
and
\omega_{2}
are distinct. The same process gives a contradiction when
\theta_{1}(P_{1})=Q_{1}
. Thus the claim follows for part (i).

By replacing
P_{1}
with
P^{\prime}_{1}
and
Q_{1}
with
Q^{\prime}_{1}
, the claim is nearly identical for part (ii). ∎

We can now conclude exactly how many such unshaded subfactor planar algebras there are. Recall that our definition of these planar algebra have no shading, so this result is not in disagreement to the result of Popa in
[
Pop94
]
.

Proof of Theorem
9.1
.

By Lemma
9.2
none of the arrow cases are isomorphic to the color cases and by Lemma
9.3
the
2n
presentations found in the arrow case and the
n
presentations found in the color case are distinct. Thus we have at least
3n
nonisomorphic unshaded subfactor planar algebras with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
.

By Theorem
6.5
and Theorem
7.12
if we have another unshaded subfactor planar algebra with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
then it must have either the arrow case presentation or the color case presentation so there are no further presentations. Thus there are exactly
3n
nonisomorphic unshaded subfactor planar algebras with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
. ∎

By following the proof with minor adjustments of Theorem
9.1
we get the following theorem.

Theorem 9.4
.

There are exactly
2n+1
nonisomorphic unshaded subfactor planar algebras with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n}
.

10
Equivalence to Cyclic Pointed Fusion Categories

Adopt the notation given for the the arrow cases of the
\tilde{A}_{2n}
and
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
unshaded subfactor planar algebras. These categories’ objects are tensor products of
Q_{1}
and
P_{1}
. Since, for
\mathcal{P}
,
Q_{1}^{\otimes(2n-1)}\cong P_{1}^{\otimes n}\otimes Q_{1}^{\otimes(n-1)}\cong P_{1}
, it is enough to say that
\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{P}}
has objects generated by
Q_{1}
(and similarly for
\mathcal{P}^{\prime})
. Let
\mathcal{C}_{m,\overline{\zeta}}
be the corresponding category that when
m=2n
is
\mathcal{P}
with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n-1}
and when
m=2n+1
is
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
with principal graph
\tilde{A}_{2n}
, with
m
th chosen root of unity
\overline{\zeta}
. In this section, we dive further into tensor categories. For more details see
[
ENO05
,
EGNO15
]
.

Recall that a
fusion
category,
\mathcal{C}
, over
\mathbb{C}
, is a rigid, semisimple,
\mathbb{C}
-linear, abelian category with only finitely many isomorphism classes of simple objects, and the unit object
\mathbb{1}
is simple. An object in a monoidal category,
\mathcal{C}
, is
invertible
if its evaluation and coevaluation maps are isomorphisms and a monoidal category
\mathcal{C}
is
pointed
if every simple object in
\mathcal{C}
is invertible.

Example 10.1
.

Let
G
be a finite group and
\omega:G\times G\times G\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{\times}
be a 3-cocycle. That is,
\omega
satisfies

\displaystyle\omega(g_{1}g_{2},g_{3},g_{4})\omega(g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}g_{4})=\omega(g_{1},g_{2},g_{3})\omega(g_{1},g_{2}g_{3},g_{4})\omega(g_{2},g_{3},g_{4})

for all
g_{1},g_{2},g_{3},g_{4}\in G
. Define
\text{Vec}_{G}^{\omega}
as the category of finite-dimensional vector spaces over
\mathbb{C}
graded by
G
with associator defined by
\omega
. That is, the simple objects are vector spaces labeled by elements of
G
,
V_{g}
, (so there is only one object in each isomorphism class) the tensor product is given by
V_{g}\otimes V_{h}=V_{gh}
, and the associativity isomorphism is determined by

\displaystyle\alpha_{V_{g},V_{h},V_{k}}=\omega(g,h,k)\text{id}_{V_{ghk}}:(V_{g}\otimes V_{h})\otimes V_{k}\to V_{g}\otimes(V_{h}\otimes V_{k})

where
g,h,k\in G
. Every pointed fusion category over
\mathbb{C}
has the form
\text{Vec}_{G}^{\omega}
for some finite group
G
and 3-cocycle
\omega

[
ENO05
]
.

A category is
strict
if the associator and both left and right unitors are the identity. For any nontrivial 3-cocycle
\omega
,
\text{Vec}_{G}^{\omega}
is not strict. The Mac Lane Strictness Theorem
[
ML98
]
states that any monoidal category is monoidally equivalent to a strict monoidal category, so we can find some strict monoidal category equivalent to
\text{Vec}_{G}^{\omega}
. In fact, for all
m\in\mathbb{N}
and associated roots of unity
\overline{\zeta}
,
\mathcal{C}_{m,\overline{\zeta}}
can easily be seen to be a strict fusion category over
\mathbb{C}
. The goal of this section then is to prove the following theorem.

Theorem 10.1
.

\mathcal{C}_{m,\overline{\zeta}}
is monoidally equivalent to
\text{Vec}_{\mathbb{Z}_{m}}^{\omega}
for some 3-cocycle
\omega
.

Through the proof of this theorem we will see how in instead of a nontrivial associator,
\omega
, of
\text{Vec}_{\mathbb{Z}_{m}}^{\omega}
, we have an on-the-nose association, at the expense of more than one object in each isomorphism class of simples.

Czenky showed in
[
Cze24
]
that the pointed fusion categories for the cyclic group
G=\mathbb{Z}_{m}
have a nice classification based on
m
roots of unity, which is denoted
\text{Vec}_{\mathbb{Z}_{m}}^{\zeta}
for chosen root of unity
\zeta
. She then gives a diagrammatic description of
\text{Vec}_{\mathbb{Z}_{m}}^{\zeta}
. Essentially, we prove Theorem
10.1
by finding a functor between
\text{Vec}_{\mathbb{Z}_{m}}^{\zeta}
and
\mathcal{C}_{m,\overline{\zeta}}
which gives an equivalence of categories. Note that the choice of
\zeta
for
\text{Vec}_{\mathbb{Z}_{m}}^{\zeta}
and
\overline{\zeta}
for
\mathcal{C}_{m,\overline{\zeta}}
is intentional as we will see that for any
m
th root of unity
\zeta
,
\text{Vec}_{\mathbb{Z}_{m}}^{\zeta}
to monoidally equivalent to
\mathcal{C}_{m,\overline{\zeta}}
where now
\overline{\zeta}
indicates complex conjugation of
\zeta
.

Fix
m\in\mathbb{Z}
and an
m
th root of unity
\zeta
. For this
\zeta
there is a 3-cocycle
\omega_{\zeta}:\mathbb{Z}_{m}\times\mathbb{Z}_{m}\times\mathbb{Z}_{m}\to\mathbb{C}^{\times}
defined by, for all
i,j,k\in\mathbb{Z}_{m}
,

\displaystyle\omega_{\zeta}(i,j,k)=\zeta^{\frac{i(j+k-[j+k])}{m}}

where
[\cdot]
indicates the value taken modulo
m
. Not only does every
m
th root of unity determine a 3-cocycle
\omega_{\zeta}
, but every 3-cocycle (modulo coboundaries) is of this form, so
\text{Vec}_{\mathbb{Z}_{m}}^{\zeta}
is defined to be
\text{Vec}_{\mathbb{Z}_{m}}^{\omega_{\zeta}}
[
Cze24
]
. In section 5 of the same paper, Czenky shows that
\text{Vec}_{\mathbb{Z}_{m}}^{\zeta}
can be given the diagrammatic description

\displaystyle\mathcal{U}

\displaystyle\mapsto\tilde{U}

\displaystyle\mathcal{U}^{*}

\displaystyle\mapsto\tilde{U}^{*}

then extend linearly and monoidally on morphisms.

Recall from the background material that
\mathcal{A}
will yield an equivalence of categories if it is full, faithful, and essentially surjective. We begin by ensuring
\mathcal{A}
is a well-defined functor.

Lemma 10.2
.

\mathcal{A}
is well-defined.

Proof.

To show the lemma, we need to prove that
\mathcal{A}
respects the defining relations of
\mathcal{D}_{m,\zeta}
. The left-hand side of relation (i) for
\mathcal{D}_{m,\zeta}
,
\mathcal{U}^{*}\mathcal{U}
maps by
\mathcal{A}
to
\tilde{U}^{*}\tilde{U}
which equals
\text{tr}(U^{*}U)=\emptyset
. As
\mathcal{A}(\text{id}_{0})=\emptyset
,
\mathcal{A}
respects relation (i).
\mathcal{F}
maps
\mathcal{U}\mathcal{U^{*}}
to
\tilde{U}\tilde{U}^{*}
. In between
U
and
U^{*}
there are oppositely oriented strands. Using the saddle relations
n
(or
n+1
, if
m
is even) times we obtain
\tilde{U}\tilde{U}^{*}=UU^{*}\otimes Q_{1}\otimes...\otimes Q_{1}
, which equals
Q_{1}^{\otimes m}
. This is the image of
\text{id}_{1}^{\otimes m}
, so
\mathcal{F}
respects relation (ii). The image of the left-hand side of relation (iii) is
Q_{1}\otimes\tilde{U}
. This equals to
\overline{\zeta}^{-1}Q_{1}\otimes\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\tilde{U})
. Then on the left-side of the diagram, there are oppositely oriented strands. Using the saddle relation we get this is equal to
\overline{\zeta}^{-1}\tilde{U}\otimes Q_{1}=\zeta\tilde{U}\otimes Q_{1}
, which is the image of the right-hand side of relation (iii). Therefore
\tilde{A}
is a well-defined functor. ∎

Lemma 10.3
.

\mathcal{A}
is essentially surjective on objects.

Proof.

As
Q_{1}
is the generating object in
\mathcal{C}_{m,\overline{\zeta}}
and the image of the generating object in
\mathcal{D}_{m,\zeta}
, the proof is immediate. ∎

To show that
\mathcal{A}
is full and faithful, we need to check that the induced map

\displaystyle\tilde{A}:\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}_{m,\zeta}}(k,\ell)\to\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}_{m,\overline{\zeta}}}\left(Q_{1}^{\otimes k},Q_{1}^{\otimes\ell}\right)

is bijective for all
k,\ell\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
. Duality allows a diagram in
\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}_{m,\zeta}}(k,\ell)
to be turned into a diagram in
\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}_{m,\zeta}}(k+\ell,0)
. Furthermore the bending of the diagram is linear and bijective, so we can equivalently prove that the induced map

\displaystyle\tilde{A}:\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}_{m,\zeta}}(k,0)\to\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}_{m,\overline{\zeta}}}\left(Q_{1}^{\otimes k},\emptyset\right)

is bijective for all
k\in\mathbb{N}
.

The hom-spaces
\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}_{m,\zeta}}(k,0)
are one-dimensional for every
k
divisible by
m
and is zero otherwise
[
Cze24
]
. If these are the dimensions of the hom-spaces
\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}_{m,\overline{\zeta}}}\left(Q_{1}^{\otimes k},\emptyset\right)
then we only need to show
\tilde{A}
is full.

Lemma 10.4
.

The dimension of
\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}_{m,\overline{\zeta}}}\left(Q_{1}^{\otimes k},\emptyset\right)
is 1 if
k
is divisible by
m
and is zero otherwise.

Proof.

Without loss of generality, suppose
m=2n+1
. The result when
k=0
was proven in Lemma
7.6
. If
0<k<n
then
Q_{1}^{\otimes k}
is a minimal projection so the hom-space is zero-dimensional. Suppose
n\leq k<2n
. Lemma
7.8
gives that
Q_{1}^{\otimes k}\cong P_{1}^{\otimes(2n-k)}
, which will be a minimal projection not isomorphic to
\emptyset
, giving again that the hom-space is zero-dimensional. If
k\geq 2n
, use the isomorphism
Q_{1}^{\otimes(2n)}\cong\emptyset
and the previous cases of
k
to get the result. ∎

Lemma 10.5
.

\mathcal{A}
is full and faithful.

Proof.

Consider the induced map
\tilde{A}:\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}_{m,\zeta}}(k,0)\to\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}_{m,\overline{\zeta}}}\left(Q_{1}^{\otimes k},\emptyset\right)
for any
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
. By Lemma
10.4
we only need to show that
\mathcal{A}
is full. The dimension of both hom-spaces are zero when
k
is not divisible by
m
, so we only need to consider when
k
is divisble by
m
. In this case, the hom-spaces are both one-dimensional, so it is enough to check the image is nontrivial. Let
k=2n\ell
for some
\ell\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
. When
\ell=0
,
\text{id}_{0}
maps to
\emptyset
, which is nontrivial as it has nonzero trace. When
\ell>0
then
\mathcal{U}^{\otimes\ell}
maps to
\tilde{U}^{\otimes\ell}
. Taking the inner product of
\tilde{U}^{\otimes\ell}
with itself is 1 and thus the image is nontrivial. ∎

Proof of Theorem
10.1
.

\mathcal{D}_{m,\overline{\zeta}}
is monoidally equivalent to
\langle Q_{1}\rangle
by Lemmas
10.2
,
10.3
, and
10.5
. The additive envelope of
\mathcal{D}_{m,\overline{\zeta}}
is monoidally equivalent to
\text{Vec}_{\mathbb{Z}_{m}}^{\zeta}
and the additive envelope of
\langle Q_{1}\rangle
is
\mathcal{C}_{m,\overline{\zeta}}
, giving the result. ∎

11
Equivalence to a Representation Category of a Finite Subgroup of
SU(2)

In a similar vein to the previous section, we show that our categories
\mathcal{C}_{m,1}
are equivalent to some diagrammatic category associated to a finite subgroup of
SU(2)
. Recall that
SU(2)
is the group of
2\times 2
matrices with entries in
\mathbb{C}
of unitary matrices with determinant 1. The Temperley-Lieb planar algebra of index 4,
\mathcal{TL}
, is equivalent to the category of finite-dimensional representations of
SU(2)
,
\text{Rep}(SU(2))
. Further, let
V=\mathbb{C}^{2}
be the defining representation of
SU(2)
and
X
a strand in
\mathcal{TL}
. Then we get an isomorphism of the hom-space
\text{Hom}(X^{\otimes k},X^{\otimes\ell})
with the space of
SU(2)
-invariant homomorphisms
\text{Hom}_{SU(2)}(V^{\otimes k},V^{\otimes\ell})
.

Finite subgroups of
SU(2)
were classified by Klein
[
Kle78
]
. McKay
[
McK80
]
showed that there is a one-to-one correspondence between the finite subgroups of
SU(2)
and the simply-laced affine Dynkin diagrams. Fix a primitive
m
th root of unity
\zeta
. Let
C_{m}^{\zeta}
be the subgroup of
SU(2)
generated by the matrix

\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\zeta&0\\
0&\zeta^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.

Define
\langle V\rangle
to be the
\mathbb{C}
-linear monoidal full subcategory generated by
V
. The representation categories of the finite subgroups of
SU(2)
are not strict, but, as done with Temperley-Lieb, our goal is to find equivalent strict monoidal categories with nice diagrammatics. To that end, we prove the following theorem:

Theorem 11.1
.

\mathcal{C}_{m,1}
is monoidally equivalent to
\text{Rep}(C_{m}^{\zeta})
.

We proceed similarly as in the previous section. Reynolds showed in
[
Rey23
]
that
\langle V\rangle
is monoidally equivalent to the following diagrammatic category, which we will call
\mathcal{B}_{m,\zeta}
. It has the following diagrammatic presentation:

then extend linearly and monoidally on morphisms.

Lemma 11.2
.

\mathcal{R}
is a well-defined functor.

Proof.

We need to check that
\mathcal{R}
respects the defining relations. Using saddle relations we see that relations (i) and (ii) are respected. Relation (iii) are the bubble relations. To see
\mathcal{R}
respects relation (iv), notice that image of the right-hand side is
Q_{1}\otimes\tilde{U}^{*}
. The top left-most strand of
\tilde{U}^{*}
and
Q_{1}
have opposite orientation, so applying the saddle relation, then the inverse of the click relation gives
\tilde{U}^{*}\otimes Q_{1}
. The same idea applies to relation (v). Relation (vi) are exactly the saddle relations. Relation (vii) is taking the trace of
UU^{*}
and
U^{*}U
. For relation (viii), the image of the left-hand side is
\tilde{U}^{\prime}\otimes\tilde{U}^{*}
. The rightmost strand of
\tilde{U}^{\prime}
and the leftmost strand of
\tilde{U}^{*}
have opposite orientation. The saddle relation then gives an equivalent diagram with a strand of
\tilde{U}^{\prime}
and
\tilde{U}^{*}
connected. Applying this
n
or
n+1
times depending on the parity of
m
, we then can apply the
U
unitary relations to get the image of the lefthand side of the relation. Relation (ix) is done the same way, so
\mathcal{R}
is well-defined. ∎

The next lemma is immediate as the two categories
\langle V\rangle
and
\langle X\rangle
each have one generating object and the image of
is
X
.

Lemma 11.3
.

\mathcal{R}
is essentially surjective on objects.

Corollary 3.6 of
[
Rey23
]
gives a basis of
\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{B}_{m,\zeta}}([k],[\ell])
. Let
\epsilon
and
\delta
be two vectors with entries
+
or
-
indicating the bottom and top boundary information of a morphism. Let
|\epsilon_{+}|
be the number of
+
labellings of
\epsilon
and similarly define
|\epsilon_{-}|
,
|\delta_{+}|
, and
|\delta_{-}|
. Define
|\epsilon|
and
|\delta|
to be the absolute value of the difference in labeling. In Lemma 3.3, Reynolds proves that
|\epsilon|\cong|\delta|(\text{mod }m)
. Reynolds also proves that any two morphisms with the same labelings are equivalent, so we can call this unique morphism
d_{\epsilon}^{\delta}
. Then the collection of these morphisms over the possible label sets form a basis of
\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{B}_{m,\zeta}}([k],[\ell])
.

We can follow the same process as in
[
Rey23
]
by noticing that the
+
that appear in coordinates of
\delta
correspond to arrows pointing in the direction of
+
and in
\epsilon
correspond to arrows pointing away from
+
. The vice versa is true for
-
. Letting now
|\epsilon_{+}|
corresponding to the number of points on the bottom boundary being the sources,
|\epsilon_{-}|
being the number of sources on the bottom boundary being the sinks,
|\delta_{+}|
being the number of points on the top boundary that are sinks and
|\delta_{-}|
being the number of points on the top boundary being the sources, we also have
|\epsilon|\equiv|\delta|(\text{mod }m)
. Further, using the exact same reasoning as his Theorem 3.5, we can conclude that any two diagrams with the same labellings (now labellings being “source” or “sink”) are equivalent. It is also clear that this unique morphism will be the image of
\mathcal{R}(d_{\epsilon}^{\delta})
. Thus the set of
\mathcal{R}(d_{\epsilon}^{\delta})
where the length of
\epsilon
is
k
and
\delta
is
\ell
form a spanning set of
\text{Hom}_{\langle X\rangle}\left(X^{\otimes k},X^{\otimes\ell}\right)
.

Lemma 11.4
.

\mathcal{R}
is full and faithful.

Proof.

As
\mathcal{R}(d_{\epsilon}^{\delta})
is a spanning set for
\text{Hom}_{\langle X\rangle}(X^{\otimes k},X^{\otimes\ell})
, we know that
\mathcal{R}
is full. Further, each
\mathcal{R}(d_{\epsilon}^{\delta})
can be split in half horizontally by construction, i.e.,
\mathcal{R}(d_{\epsilon}^{\delta})
can be written as the product of two morphisms say
fg
. Then
f^{*}fgg^{*}
is a product where all caps are multiplied by cups and all
U
multiplied by some
U^{*}
, which all evaluate to 1. So
f^{*}fgg^{*}
can be seen to be a tensor product of
P_{1}
and
Q_{1}
. The trace of this morphism is 1 so
fg=\mathcal{R}(d_{\epsilon}^{\delta})
is nonzero. Further, if
\epsilon,\epsilon^{\prime},\delta,\delta^{\prime}
are labellings of boundary data and either
\epsilon\neq\epsilon^{\prime}
or
\delta\neq\delta^{\prime}
then
\mathcal{R}(d_{\epsilon}^{\delta})
and
\mathcal{R}(d_{\epsilon^{\prime}}^{\delta^{\prime}})
live in two different hom-spaces in the planar algebra, which is graded by the boundary data. Thus the collection of
\mathcal{R}(d_{\epsilon}^{\delta})
where
\epsilon
is boundary data of length
k
and
\delta
is boundary data of length
\ell
form a basis of
\text{Hom}_{\langle X\rangle}\left(X^{\otimes k},X^{\otimes\ell}\right)
. Therefore
\mathcal{R}
is faithful.
∎

Proof of Theorem
11.1
.

\langle X\rangle
is monoidally equivalent to
\mathcal{B}_{m,\zeta}
which in
[
Rey23
]
is shown to be monoidally equivalent to
\langle V\rangle
. Taking the Cauchy completion gives the result. ∎
